While he hasn’t explicitly said the change is tied to his reelection campaign this November, the pause is expected to last through the election. As dramatic as Abbott’s about-face has been, he’s not alone: Democrats and Republicans alike are following suit. Jeremy Merrill , a data reporter at the Washington Post, analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see what elected officials on both sides of the aisle are saying about data centers. He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about his findings, what they say going into midterm elections, and how the backlash might change the way we think about what politicians owe to their constituents. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

What did you find? Data centers didn’t used to be a big deal. And now, almost all of a sudden, they’re a big issue. Candidates are falling over themselves to sound tough about data centers. And data centers are overwhelmingly portrayed as a problem rather than an opportunity or a benefit. A great example is Sen. Jon Husted, who’s a Republican senator from Ohio, who’s up for election this November. He used to praise data center projects that were coming to Ohio when he was lieutenant governor because it would help establish Ohio as “an important tech hub in America.” He said that data centers are essential to our digital lives. And now he’s saying he’s trying to “protect Americans from having to foot the bill for data centers.” He’s really emblematic of a shift that happened all across the Republican Party in about February of this year. That’s when the bulk of messages from Republicans about data centers flipped from focusing on them as bringing benefits to their states and communities, to talking about their downsides. This is really a case of the anger and unhappiness bubbling up from everyday people up to political elites. And that grassroots anger was all across the political spectrum over a whole range of issues: power bills, claims about how much water data centers may use, air pollution, eminent domain, taxes, subsidies, and a generalized, physical manifestation of the anxiety that people feel about what AI is going to do to our society, to our brains, to our kids and to our jobs. We know that it’s not just one single candidate, maybe even not just a handful, because you reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that, “Data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.” That’s pretty strong language. Is the National Republican Senatorial Committee admitting that the wrong position on data centers is enough to lose a candidate a race at this point? I think it’s something that they’re certainly worried about. He’s in a tough race. It’s a tossup . And presumably you’re looking for an edge, or to prevent your opponent from getting an edge over you. What about President Donald Trump’s messaging on data centers? He, initially at least, was very bullish on AI investment in the US. What has Trump been saying? This is a story in two or three parts. As President Trump took office again last year, he was overall trying to portray his second term as president as “inaugurating a golden age for American manufacturing and technological dominance.” As part of that, he issued an executive order trying to make it easier to build data centers in the United States. And I think that’s probably why last year most Republicans across the board were talking about data centers as a benefit to the country and to the communities where they were being built — talking about jobs, talking about investment. But like I said, the tide turned. And so on the one hand, you have President Trump promoting this bill that would protect people from having data centers cause their power bills to go up. But on the other hand, he just wrote earlier this week on Truth Social, “If [communities] want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” He’s saying if they don’t want data centers, they’re going to “end up being backwards and poor.” So he’s still very pro-data center, which is fascinating. Let’s talk about the Democrats. Which Democrats in particular are we seeing change their minds? There are a lot of governors who used to be very positive on data centers in their states because these bring jobs. These bring construction investments, some amount of permanent jobs, some amount of construction jobs. Examples of folks who are now limiting data centers in their states include Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and [Gov.] J.B. Pritzker of Illinois. The most striking case of a Democrat whose rhetoric has shifted so much is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, whose district actually includes Silicon Valley. In 2025, he was calling for building more data centers in the United States versus overseas. When the Trump administration did an AI deal with the United Arab Emirates, he said, “Why are we putting data centers and research hubs in Dubai?” But now he’s more critical, calling for an end to data center extraction, taking communities’ water and jacking up their bills, sucking all the money into the hands of a few tech billionaires. Is anyone in either party still coming out strong for data centers? My favorite example of this is Rep. Eric Burlison, who’s a Republican from Missouri. He’s really focused on the need to build data centers in order to compete with China. In June, he wrote, “Ask yourself who benefits when Americans turn against data centers? China does.” He’s making the point that I think a lot of people in tech are making, which is, “This is coming whether you like it or not.” And part of politics is dealing with reality. In this day and age, it seems constituents don’t want to deal with that reality, but clearly there are people who hold office, or who hope to hold office, who are going to maintain the line that this is something we’ve just got to do. This is a classic political science dispute about what a politician’s job is supposed to be. If you accept the premise that we need data centers to build a wonderful technological future or keep pace with China or whatever the argument is, is the job of a politician to just do what their constituents want, to be their tribune in Washington? Or is it to be the wise, thoughtful leader who’s willing to push back when constituents are missing something important? This is one thing I keep in mind when analyzing — particularly some of these governors who shifted more recently — is that they’re talking about the downsides of data centers. They’re talking about mitigating those downsides. They’re saying, “Oh, we need to get data centers to pay their fair share. We need to make sure that data centers don’t screw up our water. We need to make sure they don’t raise your power bills. We need to make sure they give back.” But then it’s so that we can build them and still reap the benefits while mitigating the costs. What is it about this issue, do you think, that has got us to this place? We’re polarized, but we’re not polarized in the same way that we’re often polarized. One possibility is that this is coming from the grassroots so much and bubbling up to politicians and political elites, that everybody got the signal at the same time that this was something that they ought to oppose. The other possibility is people have for a while been saying, “Are we living through a generational political realignment in the United States where a lot of things are up for grabs?” You don’t see a lot of the libertarian-adjacent pro-business, free markets, free trade Republican Party. And so when all these issues are up for grabs, politicians see opportunity in being innovative rather than sticking with the same traditional views of their party. ##段落
播客数据中心正将美国人团结在一起，而政客们却避之唯恐不及。作者：Ariana Aspuru 和 Noel King，2026年9月7日，上午10:00 UTC。礼品。2026年7月27日，抗议者在得克萨斯州奥斯汀的州议会大厦前集会反对数据中心。Jay Janner/《奥斯汀美国政治家报》通过Getty Images提供。数据中心引发的反弹已进入中期选举议题。过去几个月里，随着公众对数据中心建设的抵制急剧升温，各派政治人物纷纷改变立场——或至少调整政策态度。一个典型例子是得克萨斯州，大约一年前，共和党州长Greg Abbott还宣称该州是“人工智能发展的中心”。如今，经过数月基层组织和公众抗议后，Abbott正推动放缓得州新数据中心的建设步伐。他已实施全州范围内的新建暂停令，等待对得州电网新增连接的审计。虽然他未明确表示这一转变与今年11月的连任竞选有关，但暂停预计将延续至选举结束。尽管Abbott的立场逆转引人注目，但他并非孤例：民主党和共和党人都在效仿。《华盛顿邮报》数据记者Jeremy Merrill分析了数千条社交媒体帖子和新闻通讯，以了解两党民选官员对数据中心的表态。他与Today, Explained联合主持人Noel King讨论了其发现、这些发现在中期选举前的意义，以及这场反弹可能如何改变我们对政客对选民责任的理解。以下是他们对话的摘录，经过编辑以更简洁清晰。完整内容请收听播客，可通过Apple Podcasts、Pandora和Spotify等平台获取Today, Explained节目。
##段落
你发现了什么？数据中心过去并不是什么大事。而现在，几乎突然之间，它们成了大问题。候选人们争相表现得对数据中心态度强硬。数据中心被压倒性地描绘成一个问题，而非机遇或益处。一个很好的例子是来自俄亥俄州的共和党参议员Jon Husted，他将在今年11月面临选举。他担任副州长时曾赞扬来到俄亥俄州的数据中心项目，称其有助于将俄亥俄州打造为“美国重要的科技中心”。他说数据中心对我们的数字生活至关重要。而现在，他却表示要“保护美国人免于为数据中心买单”。他非常典型地反映了今年2月左右共和党内部发生的整体转变。那正是共和党人关于数据中心的大部分言论开始转向的时候。

各地关注的焦点从数据中心为州和社区带来的好处，转向了其负面影响。这实际上是普通民众的不满情绪向上蔓延至政治精英层的典型案例。这种草根阶层的愤怒跨越了整个政治光谱，涉及一系列问题：电费账单、数据中心可能消耗的水资源、空气污染、土地征用、税收、补贴，以及人们对人工智能将对社会、大脑、孩子和就业造成何种影响的普遍焦虑，这种焦虑在物理层面得到了具体体现。我们知道这不仅仅涉及某一位候选人，甚至可能不止少数几位，因为你报道过共和党参议院全国委员会警告称：“数据中心是挂在赫斯特德脖子上的锚。”这是相当强硬的措辞。共和党参议院全国委员会是否在承认，目前对数据中心的错误立场足以让候选人输掉一场竞选？我认为这肯定是他们担忧的问题。他正面临一场艰难的竞选，胜负难料。想必你是在寻找优势，或防止对手获得优势。那唐纳德·特朗普总统在数据中心问题上的表态如何？他至少最初对美国人工智能投资非常乐观。特朗普说了什么？这是一个分两三个部分的故事。随着特朗普总统去年再次上任，他总体上试图将第二任期描绘为“开启美国制造业和技术主导的黄金时代”。为此，他发布了一项行政命令，试图简化在美国建设数据中心的过程。我认为这可能是去年大多数共和党人普遍将数据中心视为对国家及建设地社区有益的原因——他们谈论就业和投资。但就像我说的，风向变了。因此，一方面，特朗普总统推动这项法案，旨在保护人们免受数据中心导致电费上涨的影响；但另一方面，他本周早些时候在Truth Social上写道：“如果（社区）想要成功和富有，拥有更低的税收和遍布各地的就业机会，就让数据为王。”他是在说，如果他们不想要数据中心，就会“最终变得落后和贫穷”。所以他仍然非常支持数据中心，这很有趣。让我们谈谈民主党人。具体有哪些民主党人改变了立场？很多州长曾经对各自州的数据中心持非常积极态度，因为这些能带来就业、建设投资、一定数量的长期职位和施工岗位。

##段落

如今在各自州内限制数据中心建设的例子包括宾夕法尼亚州州长乔什·夏皮罗和伊利诺伊州州长J.B.普里茨克。最引人注目的民主党人言辞转变案例是加利福尼亚州的众议员罗·卡纳，他的选区实际上包括硅谷。2025年，他曾呼吁在美国本土而非海外建设更多数据中心。当特朗普政府与阿联酋达成人工智能协议时，他说：“为什么我们要把数据中心和研究中心放在迪拜？”但现在他变得更加批判，呼吁终结数据中心的“榨取”行为——这些设施占用社区水资源、推高居民账单，并把所有资金吸进少数科技亿万富翁的口袋。两党中还有谁在坚定支持数据中心吗？我最喜欢的例子是密苏里州的共和党众议员埃里克·伯利森。他非常关注为了与中国竞争而建设数据中心的必要性。今年6月，他写道：“问问自己，当美国人反对数据中心时，谁受益了？是中国。”他提出的观点，我认为也是科技界许多人在强调的，即“无论你喜不喜欢，这都会到来。”而政治的一部分就是面对现实。在当今时代，选民似乎不愿接受这一现实，但显然仍有在任者或希望上任的人会坚持认为这是我们必须要做的事。这是一个经典的政治学争论，关于政治家的职责到底是什么。如果你接受我们需要数据中心来打造美好科技未来或跟上中国步伐这一前提——无论论据是什么——那么政治家的职责是仅仅听从选民的意愿，做他们在华盛顿的代言人？还是做一个明智、深思熟虑的领导者，愿意在选民忽视重要事项时提出反驳？这是我在分析时始终牢记的一点——特别是那些最近转变态度的州长——他们现在谈论的是数据中心的负面影响，谈论如何缓解这些负面影响。他们说：“哦，我们需要让数据中心支付公平份额。我们需要确保数据中心不破坏我们的水资源。我们需要确保它们不抬高你的电费。我们需要确保它们回馈社区。”但这样做是为了我们仍能建设它们，在减轻成本的同时享受收益。你认为，这个问题究竟为何让我们走到了这一步？我们处于两极分化状态，但我们的分化方式与通常看到的不同。一种可能是，这种情绪来自基层，不断向上涌动到政治家和政治精英那里，以至于每个人都

与此同时，这也传递出一个信号，表明他们应当反对此事。另一种可能性是，人们一段时间以来一直在问：“我们是否正经历美国政治格局的代际重组，许多事情都悬而未决？”你很少看到与自由意志主义相邻的亲商业、支持自由贸易的共和党。因此，当所有这些议题悬而未决时，政客们看到的是创新的机会，而非固守其政党的传统观点。查看更多：人工智能创新 2026年中期选举 播客 政治 科技 今日解析播客 用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下头脑 数据中心正将美国人团结在一起 播客 你的食物可能是安全的。但它的包装又是另一回事。我的学生认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们发现了什么。一位福音派人士解释人们对她的信仰的误解 电子邮件（必填） 注册 提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: The retro tool for stranded astronauts
body: 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sophie Hardach An old seafaring instrument could help astronauts on ever more far-flung and perilous missions. Imagine you're an astronaut flying to Mars. Suddenly, disaster strikes: all your electronic navigation systems fail. How do you find your way back home? For Nasa astronauts, the answer could be a wayfinding tool invented around 300 years ago: the sextant . Used by seafarers on Earth, and astronauts on early Nasa missions, sextants are a last-resort navigation option for missions to the Moon, and potentially, beyond – in case the high-tech ones fail. Traditionally, sextants are used to measure the angle between celestial bodies such as stars and planets, to calculate one's own position. Apart from emergency use, these ancient star-sighting skills are also attracting increased interest from Nasa engineers as humans plan to venture to Mars and beyond. "The further and further we go out, the less and less we can rely on some of the Earth-based navigation technology," such as satellites, says Greg Holt, the navigation system manager for the Orion Spacecraft and its Artemis missions to the Moon. "And so you now have to fall back more and more on what I would call the classical navigation techniques. And some of those now harken back to the way navigation was done way back in the 16th, 17th, 18th Centuries," he explains.  In that age of classical navigation, "you actually had to look at the stars to figure out where you were, and figure out your orientation relative to those celestial bodies," he says. These are skills that can be crucial in deep space "because those are some of the only references you have once you get far away from Earth". In addition, knowing how to navigate by the stars can save lives, he points out: "We want to make sure that [the astronauts] have a way to safely navigate their way back home, if for some reason they lose communication with the Earth". In 2018, Holt and his team asked two astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS), Serena Auñón-Chancellor and Alexander Gerst, to test a hand-held sextant, taking measurements with the naked eye and a steady hand. "We had crew members demonstrate the use of a manual sextant, as an emergency means of back-up navigation to get the crew home from the Moon, if they had in fact lost communication," says Holt. "Because if you lose communication, you also lose that radio navigation link with the Earth, and you're on your own at that point." The experiment tapped deep into navigational history. In the 1960s, Nasa adapted ancient star-sighting methods to space flight, though initially astronauts were not entirely sure this would work. Neil Armstrong , the first man on the Moon, recalled that "one of the things that I was concerned with at the time was whether our navigation was sufficiently accurate [...] if we lost communication with Earth, for whatever reason, could we navigate by ourselves using celestial navigation? We thought we could, but these were undemonstrated skills." The answer was yes – he and other astronauts on those early flights did successfully use sextants and other naked-eye sighting methods, both routinely, and during emergencies. Buzz Aldrin resorted to a hand-held sextant and chart during the Gemini XII spaceflight in 1966, due to a problem with the radar. And during the near-disastrous Apollo 13 flight in 1970, Jim Lovell famously used the sight of the Earth on the last stretch to get home. During the Artemis II mission to the Moon, a hand-held emergency sextant like the one Holt demonstrated was kept ready during pre-launch The 2018 experiment with the sextant on the ISS was also successful. The results were accurate enough to suggest that navigating by hand-held sextant could get the crew back home in an emergency. And the astronauts reported that they found the sextant comfortable to use in microgravity – more so than using it on Earth, in fact. Speaking by video call from Houston, Holt holds up a black sextant – essentially, the same age-old tool used by seafarers, with some small modifications for space. Its edges have been rounded off, for example, to prevent it accidentally scraping something. And it has a hook-and-loop fastener to attach it to the wall of the spacecraft, and prevent it from floating around in microgravity. Other than that, it's exactly the same device you'd find on board a normal ship on an Earthly ocean, Holt says. On the Orion spacecraft, astronauts use a high-tech version of a sextant – an optical navigation system – as a first back-up if other navigation systems fail. A camera attached to the spacecraft takes images of the surrounding stars and planets, "doing all of the same things that a crew member would be doing with the sextant", Holt says. Using image-processing techniques, the camera takes measurements such as the angles between stars, the angles between stars and planets, and the diameter of a planet. The readings are then used to automatically calculate course-corrections, for example. "On the Orion spacecraft, the Optical Navigation system serves as a back-up, providing onboard navigation capability if communication and ground-based navigation support from Earth is lost," says Holt. During the Artemis missions, the system is routinely activated about once per day. "This allows us to confirm the system remains working and healthy, [to] collect valuable imagery and performance data for our engineering design team," he says. It is also "a cross-check confirmation of the navigation solution from the Earth-based tracking".  But if this high-tech system fails, the hand-held sextant comes in.  During the Artemis II mission to the Moon in April, a hand-held emergency sextant like the one Holt demonstrated was kept ready during pre-launch, he says. If there had been a problem with the cameras of the high-tech system at that point, the sextant would have been put on board at the last minute. It is not routinely packed on Orion, as it's not necessary equipment: "Every gram of mass counts when flying space missions," he points out.  If a disastrous systems failure happens after the launch, in space, the astronauts therefore won't have that hand-held sextant on board. But they are trained to know other naked-eye methods, Holt explains. One is to look for timings of when specific stars disappear behind the Earth, or the Moon, as a rough indicator of one's own position. To me, part of the fascination of my job is seeing how all of these techniques are all interrelated – Greg Holt Holt says familiarity with the original tool is useful for Nasa's engineers, too. When leading the teams that develop the high-tech systems, "I make sure they all go out and practice with a sextant so they understand basics where all this is coming from, the maths and geometry," he says. There are also other timeless navigational tricks that help modern-day astronauts. For example, the bright, easily recognisable stars and constellations that have historically guided seafarers, are also useful navigational points for astronauts in space, says Holt. That's because they are easy to spot and recognise by humans – whether those humans are on Earth, or in a spacecraft. More like this: • What happens when astronauts get stuck in space • Should astronauts abandon the ISS? • The switch that saved a Moon mission For Mars missions, those navigational points may include asteroids, Holt says. "We would say [to the astronaut], we expect that the asteroid is going to be half-way between the two head stars in Gemini , so look over there, find that asteroid between those two stars, take your readings, then compare that against the expectations and do the maths." If the readings are off, the astronauts correct the course to get to where they want to be. "To me, part of the fascination of my job is seeing how all of these techniques are all interrelated, from the earliest forms of star sightings off ships, all the way to how we're looking to navigate off to Mars and even further places," says Holt. Even the most far-flung missions still involve the same fundamental concepts, he says: looking at stars, looking at objects in comparison to the stars, and using geometric relationships to determine where we are. "Whether we are doing it manually with a stick, or a sextant, or a high-tech camera, it's fascinating to me that a lot of these same techniques are all linked and have those common heritages and mathematical foundations." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.    For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram . 4天前 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 苏菲·哈达克 一件古老的航海仪器可能帮助宇航员执行日益遥远和危险的 missions。想象你是一名飞往火星的宇航员。突然，灾难降临：所有电子导航系统失灵。你如何找到回家的路？对于NASA宇航员来说，答案可能是一种约300年前发明的定位工具：六分仪。六分仪曾被地球上的海员和早期NASA任务的宇航员使用，是前往月球及更远任务中的最后备用导航选项，以防高科技系统失效。传统上，六分仪用于测量恒星和行星等天体之间的角度，以计算自身位置。除了应急用途，随着人类计划向火星及更远地区探险，这些古老的观星技能也日益引起NASA工程师的兴趣。

##段落 猎户座飞船及其阿尔忒弥斯月球任务的导航系统经理格雷格·霍尔特表示：“我们走得越远，就越不能依赖某些基于地球的导航技术，”如卫星。“因此，你现在必须越来越多地依赖我所谓的经典导航技术。其中一些技术现在可以追溯到16、17、18世纪的导航方式。”他解释说，在那个经典导航时代，“你实际上必须观察星星来确定自己的位置，并弄清自己相对于这些天体的方向。”这些技能在深空中可能至关重要，“因为一旦远离地球，这些是你仅有的参照物之一。”此外，他指出，懂得如何通过星星导航可以挽救生命：“我们希望确保（宇航员）有办法安全导航回家，以防他们因某种原因与地球失去通信。”

##段落 2018年，霍尔特和他的团队要求国际空间站（ISS）上的两名宇航员塞雷娜·奥尼翁-钱塞勒和亚历山大·格斯特测试一种手持六分仪，用肉眼和稳定手部进行测量。霍尔特说：“我们让机组人员演示了手动六分仪的使用，作为从月球返回地球的应急备用导航手段，如果他们确实失去通信的话。”“因为如果你失去通信，你也会失去与地球的无线电导航链接，那时你只能靠自己。”这项实验深入挖掘了导航历史。在1960年代，NASA将古老的观星方法应用于太空飞行，尽管最初宇航员并不完全确定这能否奏效。第一个登上月球的人尼尔·阿姆斯特朗回忆说，“我担心的事情之一

当时的问题是，我们的导航是否足够精确[...]如果因为任何原因与地球失去通信，我们能否依靠自己使用天体导航来导航？我们认为可以，但这些技能尚未得到验证。”答案是肯定的——他和早期那些飞行任务中的其他宇航员确实成功使用了六分仪和其他裸眼观测方法，既用于常规操作，也用于紧急情况。巴兹·奥尔德林在1966年的双子座十二号太空飞行中，由于雷达出现问题，他求助于手持六分仪和星图。而在1970年近乎灾难性的阿波罗13号飞行中，吉姆·洛弗尔著名地利用地球的视线完成了最后一段返航路程。在阿尔忒弥斯二号月球任务中，像霍尔特演示的那种手持应急六分仪在发射前一直保持就绪状态。2018年在国际空间站上使用六分仪的实验也取得了成功。结果足够精确，表明在紧急情况下，使用手持六分仪导航可以让机组人员返回地球。宇航员还报告说，他们发现六分仪在微重力环境中使用起来很舒适——实际上比在地球上使用时更舒适。通过休斯敦的视频通话，霍尔特举起一个黑色六分仪——本质上，这是与航海者使用的古老工具相同的设备，只是做了一些细微的太空改造。例如，它的边缘已被磨圆，以防止意外刮擦其他物体。它还配有魔术贴，可将其固定在航天器壁上，防止它在微重力中漂浮。除此之外，它与普通船只在地球海洋上使用的设备完全相同，霍尔特说。在猎户座航天器上，宇航员使用高科技版本的六分仪——一种光学导航系统——作为其他导航系统失效时的第一备用方案。航天器上附带的摄像头拍摄周围恒星和行星的图像，“执行与机组人员使用六分仪时相同的所有功能”，霍尔特说。利用图像处理技术，摄像头测量诸如恒星之间的角度、恒星与行星之间的角度以及行星直径等参数。然后，这些读数被用于自动计算航线修正，例如。“在猎户座航天器上，光学导航系统作为备用方案，如果与地球的通信和地基导航支持丢失，它提供机载导航能力，”霍尔特说。在阿尔忒弥斯任务期间，该系统大约每天例行激活一次。“这使我们能够确认系统保持运行和健康，[并]为我们的工程设计团队收集宝贵的图像和性能数据，”他说。它也是对来自地基跟踪的导航解决方案的“交叉检查确认”。

但如果这一高科技系统出现故障，手持式六分仪便会派上用场。霍尔特表示，在四月份的“阿耳忒弥斯二号”探月任务中，他演示的那种手持式应急六分仪在发射前一直保持备用状态。若当时高科技系统的摄像头出现问题，六分仪便会在最后一刻被装上飞船。它并非“猎户座”飞船的常规配备，因为并非必需设备：“执行太空任务时，每一克质量都至关重要，”他指出。因此，若发射后在太空中发生灾难性系统故障，宇航员手边不会有那台手持式六分仪。但霍尔特解释说，他们受过训练，掌握其他裸眼观测方法。一种方法是通过观察特定恒星消失在地球或月球背后的时间，作为自身位置的大致指标。霍尔特说，对原始工具的熟悉对NASA工程师也大有裨益。在带领团队开发高科技系统时，“我确保他们都出去用六分仪实践，以便理解这一切所基于的基础——数学和几何学，”他说。还有其他永恒不衰的导航技巧能帮助现代宇航员。例如，历史上指引航海者的明亮、易识别的恒星和星座，也对太空中的宇航员构成有用的导航参照点，霍尔特说。这是因为它们易于人类目视发现和辨认——无论这些人类身处地球还是航天器中。更多类似内容：• 宇航员被困太空时会发生什么• 宇航员是否应放弃国际空间站• 拯救登月任务的开关对于火星任务，这些导航点可能包括小行星，霍尔特说。“我们会（对宇航员）说，我们预计这颗小行星将位于双子座两颗主星正中间，所以看向那边，找到那颗位于两星之间的小行星，进行读数，然后与预期对比，并做数学计算。”若读数有偏差，宇航员便修正航向，以抵达目标位置。“对我而言，我工作的一大魅力在于看到所有这些技术如何相互关联，从船上最早的观星形式，一直到我们如何导航前往火星甚至更远的地方，”霍尔特说。即使是距离最远的任务，也仍涉及相同的基本原理，他说：观测恒星，将天体与恒星对比观察，并利用几何关系来确定我们所处的位置。“无论我们是手持木棍、六分仪还是高科技摄像头手动操作，这都让我着迷。”

许多这类技术都有共通之处，并共享着相同的历史渊源与数学基础。”——若您喜欢这篇报道，欢迎订阅《要闻精选》新闻信——每周两次为您奉上精心挑选的特稿、视频及不容错过的新闻资讯。欲获取更多来自BBC的科学、科技、环境与健康故事，请关注我们的Facebook和Instagram账号。太空 宇航员 太阳系 科学 天文学 火星 月球 技术 数学 特辑

readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

Excerpted from The Song of Significance: A New Manifesto for Teams by Seth Godin, in agreement with Portfolio, an imprint of Penguin Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC. Copyright © Seth Godin 2023.

about work. His books have been translated into 38 languages. Godin writes one of the most popular marketing blogs in the world, and his TED talks are among the most popular of all time. He is the founder of the altMBA, the social media pioneer Squidoo, and Yoyodyne, one of the first internet companies. Find out more at seths.blog.

readings.cn:
让我们别再称其为“软技能”——而应改称“真实技能”

2023年6月9日 / 赛斯·戈丁 / Facebook X LinkedIn Reddit WhatsApp 黛博拉·斯皮尔曼

我们仍在像经营保龄球队一样进行招聘和培训，仿佛只有易于衡量的技能才至关重要。

是什么导致成功组织走向失败？是什么让股票黯然失色、创新放缓、客户流失？我们都能认同某些技能不可或缺。雇佣不会编程的程序员、不会销售的销售员、或不会设计的建筑师，无疑是浪费。但这些技能——我们不妨称之为职业技能——已成为招聘流程的核心支柱。

但如何解释相似的组织，拥有同样职业技能出众的人才，却面临截然不同的结果？学生体验的大多数教科书和参加的考试，都聚焦于职业技能，即求职所需勾选的清单。通过错误定义“职业性”并过度聚焦于这些所谓的关键技能，我们贬低了其他真正重要的技能的价值。

当我们称其他技能为“软”技能，暗示它们是可有可无时，我们给予了它们过少的尊重。真正区分繁荣组织与挣扎组织的，是难以衡量的态度、流程以及从业者的认知。

职业技能可以传授：你不是天生就懂工程、文案写作甚至平面设计，因此它们必然是能教会的。但在决策、积极参与、与恐惧共舞、权威发言、团队协作、洞察真相、直言不讳、激励他人、超越分内之事、用心关怀以及勇于变革这些方面，我们却让自己轻易脱身。我们在此类培训上投入不足，担心这些特质是与生俱来、无法传授的。或许它们是天赋。于是我们轻描淡写，称其为软技能，让自己得以转向看似更紧迫的事务。

在规模化层面，组织在招聘时对软技能的关注度较低，因为我们说服自己相信职业技能是非个人化、更易衡量的。若某项技能更易测试，在选拔团队时似乎就更重要。

当这些技能缺失时，我们却迟迟不采取行动（也很少再培训），因为我们担心踩到他人痛处，担心被指责过于个人化，或担心在无望之事上浪费时间。

但这些技能全都可以习得，就像下棋或打字这类显而易见的技能一样。我们通过偶然、耳濡目染、以及与教师、父母、老板和世界的碰撞中学会它们。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们无法提升它们、无法加以练习。

我们不能改变我们的工作方式吗？  
我们当然可以。  
让我们别再称它们为“软技能”了。它们是人际技能，是领导技能，是魅力、勤奋和贡献的技能。但这些修饰词，虽然准确，却不知怎地把它们从职业技能、从我们实际招聘所依据的技能、从我们衡量研究生学位的技能中排挤开来。  
所以，让我们不自在地把它们称为“真实技能”吧。  
真实，因为它们行之有效，因为它们是当今我们所需的核心。  
真实，因为即使你拥有职业技能，若没有这些人类技能——那些我们无法写下来或编程让计算机去做的事情——你对我们也毫无帮助。  
真实技能当然无法取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经衡量的那些东西。  
想象一个拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、熟练、经验丰富。一份能证明这一切的简历。那是一个不错的基线。  
现在，在此基础上添加：敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、目标明确、鼓舞人心且积极主动。慷慨、富有同理心且始终如一。一个耐心的深度倾听者。当这样的人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么变化？  
在《哈佛商业评论》中撰文时，娄·所罗门报道称，69%的经理人对与员工沟通感到不自在。我猜想，另外31%中的许多人都在撒谎。  
与员工沟通之所以令人不适，是因为我们构建了顺从和支配的系统，使其变得困难。我们要求人们将人性留在门外，然后用权威来改变行为。我们将企业贪婪和短期思维与创造有意义工作的人类渴望叠加在一起。  
我们如何建立以人为本的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的经理人（想必薪酬丰厚、训练有素且对我们的成功不可或缺）对执行其工作的基本部分感到如此不适，以至于他们向陌生人承认了这一点？  
在最近一项调查中，研究生入学管理委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、量化专长和信息收集能力方面表现强劲，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面和口头沟通、领导力和适应性。这些是相互排斥的吗？我们必须以牺牲一方来换取另一方吗？  
所有真实技能的基础是这一条：拥有相互交谈的自信和许可。不是去管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。仅仅是寻求被理解，并努力去理解他人。  
摘自赛斯·高汀的《意义之歌：团队新宣言》，经Portfolio出版社（企鹅兰登书屋旗下品牌）同意使用。

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 社交媒体平台曾经是朋友之间交流的工具——如今，许多平台正日益变成短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式就是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并提高广告收入。但消费者是否已经开始产生抵触情绪？

##段落

奥蕾莉亚给自己冲了一杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近美丽的花园里，打开Instagram“放松一下”。首先映入眼帘的是：“一个我非常喜欢的室内设计师。他现在在威尼斯。”她热衷于室内设计，甚至刚刚把19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的两幅鸟类画作纹在了手臂上。她继续往下滑动。两只小猫在打架。“我喜欢动物，所以我会看到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，他们就给你推送香蕉。”也有广告——尽管看起来和其他帖子没什么两样——比如扫地机器人、减肥餐和带有莫里斯风格图案的床品。但没有朋友的内容。她在Instagram上有198个好友，但她说“情况完全变了。我几乎再也看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她自己基本上也不再发帖了。“我觉得反正也没人看了。”

##段落

尽管在Instagram，尤其是Facebook上，仍然有一批忠实的、以社交为目的的业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览陌生人的专业制作内容，这一趋势在年轻用户中尤为明显。16岁的基利安正在接受厨师职业培训。他说自己经常刷TikTok和YouTube。“我喜欢看视频胜过看照片或消息。我看的是不认识的人制作的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的小圈子里。我只是看，仅此而已。我把自己的反应藏在心里。”

##段落

“我花很多时间刷内容创作者制作的视频，”同样16岁的露西说。“它们比我认识的人发的帖子更有趣。”她自己不发帖，只是偶尔发一些24小时后就会消失的“快拍”。无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们早已远离了社交媒体几年前还是“数字城市广场”式的个人互动时代。在法国，2026年官方年度《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“只是偶尔活跃”。在英国，4月份发布的一份Ofcom报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比下降，从61%降至49%。在美国，去年6月Morning Consult的一项调查发现，28%的受访者表示发帖频率比前一年减少了。目前只有33%的人每天发帖，而每天使用社交媒体进行娱乐的人则占57%。在Z世代中，这一差距更为悬殊——18%为活跃用户，74%为被动用户。瓦内莎·拉洛是巴黎一位专攻网络行为研究的临床心理学家。

她说：“用户已经越来越意识到，你在社交媒体上留下的痕迹会永远存在，一些人不再想维持可能肤浅的社交媒体关系。有些人不想暴露在发帖时可能面临的批评风险中，或者感觉自己的帖子在众多专业内容旁边显得逊色。”然而，拉洛补充道，人们并没有停止发帖，而是开始发布不同的内容，并在不同的平台上发布。“例如，在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是有趣的恶搞和现有素材的混剪。目标是让人们发笑，而不是讲述自己的生活。”她说，这种分享生活的内容仍然存在，但已经从Instagram和Facebook等社交媒体平台转移到了WhatsApp等即时通讯应用上。此外，人们也开始转向Instagram和Snapchat上的私密群组。“这些是更加私密的空间，你不会被广告和网红内容轰炸，”她说。

##段落
社交媒体顾问、Geekout新闻通讯作者马特·纳瓦拉表示：“我们正在看到社交媒体一分为二。Instagram和TikTok等大型平台正变得更加注重娱乐和发现。WhatsApp正成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题是，这类空间更难让公司从中获利。”小企业主正被推着成为主持人、编辑、潮流发现者和内容创作者，同时还要实际经营业务——马特·纳瓦拉正是TikTok率先推出了这种算法，它能从你开始滑动屏幕的那一刻就判断出你喜欢什么，然后填满你的信息流，让你尽可能长时间地留在应用上。现在，马特·纳瓦拉说：“Meta已在Facebook和Instagram上构建了所谓的不相关内容的AI推荐系统，这基本上意味着，平台越来越多地向你展示你不关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向于判断内容是专业创作者、品牌还是朋友制作的。如果它发现你和某个朋友互动很多，你可能会看到更多他们的内容。只是你与谁是朋友、你关注了谁，在某种程度上已经变得无关紧要了。”这一切都意味着，长期利用社交媒体进行免费推广的小企业必须提升自己的水平。

##段落
马特·纳瓦拉说：“对于一些小企业来说，确实存在真正的机会。一家面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，如果他们有好的故事、有吸引力的视觉效果或人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以脱颖而出。但这也意味着工作方式已经改变。小企业主正被推着成为主持人、编辑、潮流发现者和内容创作者，同时还要实际经营业务。”

##段落
实际上运营业务的顶端。"社交平台继续主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这仍然是核心商业模式，而广告收入也在持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉说。

##段落
社交媒体正在演变成类似于电视的被动媒介，尽管是那种在你切换频道时会自我调整的电视。或者更确切地说，它对你了解得太深，以至于它拿走了遥控器这件事似乎也不那么重要了。你向平台提供关于自己的信息，平台利用这些信息获取商业利益，作为回报，它免费为你提供量身定制、取悦你的内容。从真正的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转型似乎确实在获得回报。"社交平台继续主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这仍然是核心商业模式，而广告收入也在持续增长，"马特·纳瓦拉表示。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将从去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）增长至2026年的3170亿美元（2360亿英镑）。

##段落
Meta是最大的赢家。其广告销售额在2025年已经同比增长了22%，预计今年将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），足以首次超越谷歌。人工智能驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得前所未有的高效和精准。"社交平台允许企业在你浏览的内容中插入广告。每滚动三四次就会出现一条广告。它们是世界上最好的广告定向引擎。它们对你的兴趣了如指掌，因为你浏览过什么、点赞过什么、互动过什么、选择关注了什么、在应用的某些区域停留了多长时间，诸如此类，"纳瓦拉说。"所以广告主会过来说：'我想把广告投放在英国30到60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人群旁边'，社交平台会掌握这些信息，并相应地投放广告。"价格取决于广告主想要的展示次数（点击量）以及筛选标准的精确程度。把广告投放在购买马匹的人群的社交媒体信息流中，比投放在购买冰淇淋的人群中成本更高。

##段落
更多相关内容：• TikTok在追踪你，即使你不使用该应用。以下是阻止方法• 如何阻止AI把你的大脑变成浆糊• 这张猴子自拍照将保护你免受AI垃圾内容的侵害

##段落
会不会有一场反弹即将到来？难道不是很多人先上社交媒体看看朋友对自己的帖子或评论有何反应，然后才安顿下来浏览专业制作的内容吗？无论是上这些应用的社交动机在减弱，还是其他原因，人们在社交媒体上花费的时间在2025年趋于平稳，平均为141分钟，比2024年的143分钟略有下降。然而，这只是故事的一部分，因为使用社交媒体的人数……

人工智能以及人类在这些应用上花费的总时间持续攀升。对于Z世代而言，这一数字更高，在美国每天大约五小时，社交媒体已成为这一群体的主要搜索引擎和购物工具。同时，对于那些怀念社交媒体能让你与熟人分享生活点滴、笑话或观点的“旧日时光”的人来说，平台内也有工具可选择主要查看朋友和家人的内容，马特·纳瓦拉指出。“人们可以切换到那样的信息流，”他说，“但大多数人不会这么做。”——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《必备清单》新闻通讯——每周两次精选特稿、视频和不容错过的新闻，直接发送至你的邮箱。欲了解更多商业及更多领域动态，请在领英上关注我们。商业科技特稿社交媒体商业世界

readings.title: Your food may be safe. Its packaging is another story.
body: Climate Your food may be safe. Its packaging is another story. A sweeping new study shows why you should ditch plastic food wrapping whenever possible. by Liza Gross Sep 7, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Gift Baby food pouches, in particular, carry a higher chemical exposure risk. Jeffrey Greenberg, Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. Most people decide if it’s safe to eat an old tub of yogurt in the fridge or canned tuna in the back of the cupboard by checking its sell-by date. But no label indicates that pesticides, phthalates, PFAS, or other hazardous chemicals could be seeping from those containers into your food. Of more than 15,000 chemicals that come in contact with food, a new peer-reviewed study found that 1,222 pose serious health risks such as cancer and reproductive harm. And the vast majority — 87 percent, or more than 13,200 — lack enough accessible information to even estimate their risks. The fact that there’s not enough publicly available information for independent scientists to assess the safety of chemicals that can contaminate food is “the elephant in the room,” said study co-author Jane Muncke, managing director at the nonprofit Food Packaging Forum Foundation, which led the research, published Tuesday in the journal Environmental Science & Technology . Consumers trust that when regulators allow chemicals in products like food packaging, it’s because it’s been through safety testing, Muncke said. “But that’s not the case,” she said. “And it doesn’t make sense.” The team has done a “very, very good job” highlighting how little is known about the risks of substances that affect everyone, said Maricel Maffini, an independent chemical safety and regulation expert who was not involved in the study but has collaborated with Muncke in the past. Because the study focused on a list that people in industry and regulators regard as reliable, it’s looking under the proverbial lamppost, Maffini said. While there’s plenty of information suggesting that many of these chemicals should not be on the market or should have stronger regulations, she said, there’s so much information beyond that list that’s missing. In previous work, Muncke and her team identified more than 15,000 chemicals used in food processing or packaging from lists of substances approved by regulators in the United States, China, Japan, and countries in Europe and South America or that had been identified in studies . In the new paper, they analyzed that “jaw-dropping” number of chemicals, Muncke said, to flag the most problematic. To maximize the utility of their priority list, the team used only data obtained from governmental and regulatory agencies linking a chemical to human health hazards such as cancer, reproductive harm, or ability to concentrate in the body. That yielded a priority list of 1,222 chemicals that they ranked into four tiers, with the highest to lowest evidence of human exposure from food-contact materials. Ninety-four chemicals known to seep into food and detected in breast milk, blood, or other human samples were assigned to Tier 1, the highest priority for regulators and companies to consider phasing out. These chemicals include liver- and immune system-damaging PFAS “forever chemicals,” which make food wrappers grease- or water-resistant; the likely carcinogen styrene , used to produce takeout packages and refrigerated dairy food containers; hormone-disrupting phthalates , added to make plastics like those that hold vegetable oils flexible; and bisphenol A, added to hard plastics and can linings and a poster child for endocrine disruptors’ ability to impair development at low doses. Studies have found these and other chemicals leaching from containers into a diverse array of food and beverages, including water, infant formula , orange juice , ice cream , yogurt and cream , oils, cake, and fatty foods . The next highest priority list, Tier 2, included an additional 264 hazardous chemicals that leach into food but have not been detected in biomonitoring studies. At least, not yet. Experts with the Food Packaging Forum say regulators can take simple steps to reduce people’s exposure to harmful chemicals found or used in food-contact materials, starting with moving away from evaluating one chemical at a time. People are exposed to multiple synthetic chemicals simultaneously through food-contact materials, textiles, personal-care products, air pollution, and more. Regulators should introduce a “mixture allocation factor,” which creates a safety margin that accounts for the combined effects of multiple chemicals in a single exposure. Chemicals should be regulated in groups. If there is sufficient evidence that individual chemicals in a group with similar structures and properties are hazardous, then all members of that group should be pulled from the market or not approved until proven safe, as the European Union did in its 2023 proposal to restrict PFAS as a group. Modify rules for material safety to ensure that what escapes from products is safe under different use conditions and expand screening of toxicity to include chronic disease outcomes like diabetes, infertility, and harm to the immune and nervous systems. Determine if chemicals or materials like glass or stainless steel classified as inert leach into food. If they don’t leach, they’re not a priority for in-depth chemical analysis. Inert materials that can be reused should be the policy goal. The chemicals in Tier 1 provide the most reliable evidence that materials that come in contact with food are a source of people’s exposure to these chemicals, Muncke said. The chemicals are in people, they’re in food, and they’re in food-contact materials, she said. “What more proof do you want?” Inside Climate News asked the American Chemistry Council and Food Packaging Coalition, trade groups that represent the chemical and food-packing industries, if their members would release hazard information about the chemicals they use and phase out those known to be hazardous. Neither responded, but the Food Packaging Coalition maintains that packaging is designed to prevent the transfer of its components to food and to ensure that they are safe and suitable for their intended use. The paper offers a practical and transparent roadmap for using the best available evidence to prioritize food-contact chemicals for regulation, said Sara Lupolt, an expert on exposure assessment at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who was not involved in the research. Though not addressed in the paper, she added, more research is needed to determine which foods and chemical combinations result in more chemicals moving into food. Many of the chemicals that migrate into food are so-called non-intentionally added substances, (NIAS). Their identity is often obscure because existing tools can’t identify every chemical in use, especially when researchers don’t know what to look for because producers keep proprietary chemical ingredients secret. Muncke is particularly concerned about babies’ exposure to plastic chemicals in pouches that hold juices and pureed food. Earlier this year, her team found evidence that more than 330 chemicals leach from pouches, including nearly 80 known to be hazardous. They presented the findings at an event at the House of Lords in the United Kingdom in June. A greater volume of chemicals gets into baby food because the ratio of packaging to food is much greater in a small serving size, Muncke said. And the pouches are sterilized using heat, which drives chemicals to migrate and forms microplastics. Several peer-reviewed studies, including a 2023 Chemosphere study , also found chemicals, including NIAS, in baby food packaged in pouches. The paper’s authors believed the NIAS, which lacked adequate information to assess risk, were impurities and raw materials from producing plastic. “Infants may be constantly exposed to NIAS via consuming pouched food products,” the authors warned. For the 87 percent of chemicals that lack hazard data, it’s primarily a question of the data not being public, said study co-author Helene Wiesinger, a chemist and Food Packaging Forum scientific officer. That delays regulatory action, Wiesinger said, because governments and independent scientists must first figure out which chemicals are safe. She believes a product or chemical should not be allowed on the market until a company can prove that it’s safe. At a minimum, chemicals that have structural similarities with others known to be hazardous should be priorities for regulation, the paper argues. Seventy percent of the more than 4,200 chemicals the team classified into 38 priority groups — including PFAS, phthalates and organophosphates (used as flame retardants and pesticides, among other applications) — lack enough data to assess potential harms. Just because something isn’t yet known to be hazardous doesn’t mean it’s not hazardous, Wiesinger said. Time and again, chemicals found to present unreasonable risks are replaced with others that have similar properties and ultimately similar risks. “We hope this work provides practical guidance on how to at least not make the very obvious mistakes,” she said. 你的食物可能是安全的，但它的包装就是另一回事了。一项广泛的新研究揭示了为什么你应该尽可能避免使用塑料食品包装。

##段落

特别是婴儿食品袋，携带更高的化学暴露风险。杰弗里·格林伯格，环球图像集团通过盖蒂图片社

##段落

本文最初由《内部气候新闻》发布，作为气候台合作的一部分在此转载。大多数人通过检查冰箱里一桶老酸奶或橱柜后面罐头金枪鱼的保质期来决定它们是否还能安全食用。但没有任何标签表明农药、邻苯二甲酸盐、全氟和多氟烷基物质或其他危险化学物质可能从这些容器渗入你的食物。一项新的同行评审研究发现，在超过15000种与食物接触的化学物质中，有1222种对健康构成严重风险，如癌症和生殖损害。而绝大多数——87%，即超过13200种——缺乏足够的可获取信息来甚至评估其风险。

##段落

事实上，没有足够的公开信息让独立科学家评估可能污染食物的化学物质的安全性，这是“房间里的大象”，该研究的合著者、非营利组织食品包装论坛基金会董事总经理简·蒙克表示。该基金会领导了这项研究，该研究于周二发表在《环境科学与技术》杂志上。蒙克说，消费者相信，当监管机构允许化学物质用于食品包装等产品时，是因为它们经过了安全测试。“但事实并非如此，”她说，“而且这说不通。”

##段落

未参与该研究但与蒙克过去有过合作的独立化学安全与监管专家马里塞尔·马菲尼表示，该团队做了一项“非常非常好的工作”，强调了人们对影响每个人的物质风险知之甚少。马菲尼说，由于这项研究聚焦于行业和监管机构认为可靠的清单，它是在众所周知的灯柱下寻找。她说，虽然有大量信息表明这些化学物质中的许多不应上市或应受到更严格的监管，但该清单之外还有大量信息缺失。

##段落

在先前的工作中，蒙克和她的团队从美国、中国、日本以及欧洲和南美洲国家的监管机构批准的清单或研究中已识别的物质中，确定了超过15000种用于食品加工或包装的化学物质。蒙克说，在新论文中，他们分析了这个“令人瞠目结舌”的化学物质数量，以标记出最成问题的物质。为了最大化其优先级清单的实用性，该团队仅使用了从政府和监管机构获得的数据，将化学物质与

某些化学物质对人体健康构成危害，如致癌、损害生殖能力或在体内积聚。由此得出一份包含1，222种化学物质的优先清单，并按人类从食品接触材料中接触到的证据强度从高到低分为四个等级。其中，已知会渗入食品并在母乳、血液或其他人体样本中检测到的94种化学物质被列为第一等级，这是监管机构和公司考虑逐步淘汰的最高优先级。这些化学物质包括损害肝脏和免疫系统的全氟烷基物质（PFAS）“永久性化学物质”，它们使食品包装纸具有防油或防水性；可能致癌的苯乙烯，用于生产外卖包装和冷藏乳制品容器；干扰内分泌的邻苯二甲酸盐，用于增加塑料（如装植物油的那些塑料）的柔韧性；以及双酚A，添加于硬塑料和罐头内衬中，是内分泌干扰物在低剂量下就能损害发育的典型代表。研究发现，这些及其他化学物质会从容器渗入多种食品和饮料中，包括水、婴儿配方奶粉、橙汁、冰淇淋、酸奶和奶油、油类、蛋糕及高脂肪食品。下一高优先级清单（第二等级）还包括另外264种会渗入食品但尚未在生物监测研究中检测到的有害化学物质——至少目前还未检测到。食品包装论坛的专家表示，监管机构可以采取简单措施减少人们接触食品接触材料中发现或使用的有害化学物质，首先从不再逐一对单一化学物质进行评估开始。人们通过食品接触材料、纺织品、个人护理产品、空气污染等多种途径同时接触到多种合成化学物质。监管机构应引入“混合物分配系数”，建立安全边际，以考虑一次接触中多种化学物质的联合效应。化学物质应按类别进行监管。如果某一结构性质相似的化学物质组中个别成员有充分证据表明具有危害性，则该组所有成员都应撤出市场或未经证明安全前不予批准，正如欧盟在2023年提议将全氟烷基物质作为一个整体加以限制那样。修改材料安全规则，确保在不同使用条件下从产品中释放的物质是安全的，并将毒性筛查扩大到包括糖尿病、不孕症以及对免疫和神经系统的损害等慢性疾病结果。确定被归类为惰性的化学物质或材料（如玻璃或不锈钢）是否会渗入食品。如果没有渗漏，就不是进行深入化学分析的重点。可重复使用的惰性材料应成为政策目标。第一等级中的化学物质提供了……

蒙克表示，有最可靠的证据表明，接触食品的材料是人们接触这些化学物质的一个来源。她说，这些化学物质存在于人体内、食品中以及食品接触材料中。“你们还想要什么证据？”Inside Climate News询问了代表化学和食品包装行业的美国化学理事会和食品包装联盟，问其成员是否会公布他们使用的化学品的危害信息，并逐步淘汰已知有害的化学品。两者均未回应，但食品包装联盟坚持认为，包装的设计是为了防止其成分转移到食品中，并确保其安全且适合预期用途。约翰斯·霍普金斯大学布隆伯格公共卫生学院的暴露评估专家萨拉·卢波尔特表示，这篇论文提供了一条实用且透明的路线图，利用现有最佳证据优先对食品接触化学品进行监管，但她未参与这项研究。她补充说，尽管论文未涉及，但仍需更多研究来确定哪些食品和化学组合会导致更多化学物质迁移到食品中。许多迁移到食品中的化学物质是所谓的非有意添加物质（NIAS）。它们的身份往往不明确，因为现有工具无法识别使用中的每种化学物质，尤其是当研究人员不知道该寻找什么时，因为生产商对专有化学成分保密。蒙克特别关注婴儿通过装有果汁和果泥的包装袋接触塑料化学品的情况。今年早些时候，她的团队发现证据表明，超过330种化学物质从包装袋中浸出，其中包括近80种已知有害物质。他们在6月于英国上议院的一次活动中展示了这些发现。蒙克说，由于小份包装中包装与食品的比例更大，因此进入婴儿食品的化学物质数量更多。而且包装袋通过加热灭菌，这会促使化学物质迁移并形成微塑料。包括2023年《Chemosphere》研究在内的几项同行评审研究也发现，装在包装袋中的婴儿食品含有包括NIAS在内的化学物质。论文作者认为，缺乏足够信息评估风险的NIAS是塑料生产中的杂质和原材料。“婴儿可能通过食用袋装食品持续暴露于NIAS，”作者警告道。对于87%缺乏危害数据的化学物质，研究合著者、化学家兼食品包装论坛科学官员海伦·维辛格表示，这主要是数据不公开的问题。维辛格说，这延迟了监管行动，因为政府和独立科学家必须

第一步是要弄清楚哪些化学物质是安全的。她认为，在产品或化学物质被允许进入市场之前，公司必须能够证明其安全性。论文指出，至少，那些与已知有害物质具有结构相似性的化学物质应优先受到监管。该团队将超过4200种化学物质分类为38个优先组别，其中包括PFAS、邻苯二甲酸盐和有机磷酸酯（用作阻燃剂和农药等），其中70%缺乏足够的数据来评估潜在危害。维辛格表示，仅仅因为某物质尚未被认定为有害，并不意味着它无害。一次又一次，被发现有不可接受风险的化学物质被替换为具有类似性质、最终带来类似风险的替代品。她说：“我们希望这项工作能提供实用指导，至少避免犯下非常明显的错误。”##段落查看更多：气候健康公共卫生科学用最新的Vox填字游戏放松一下数据中心正在将美国人团结在一起播客一位福音派人士解释了人们对她的信仰的误解一个家伙制作了一个深度伪造应用，将女性照片变成裸体。结果并不顺利。我的学生认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们说得有道理。邮箱（必填）注册提交您的邮箱即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: How to future-proof your wrists
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google David Cox Modern life is ruining our wrists. We can all do something about it, but it helps to start early. It began with a dull ache. Over the course of a summer, it rapidly progressed to an arm-juddering pain, radiating through my left hand every time I struck a tennis ball or even attempted to open a door. I was 18 at that point, and playing competitive tennis was an important part of my life, but I'd just experienced an injury that would plague me for years. Now, nearly two decades later, it could increase my risk of developing wrist arthritis. Such problems are surprisingly common in mid to later life.  Our wrists are remarkably adaptable. They have the strength to allow us to lift heavy objects (including the World Record of  2,422 kg (5339 lbs) ), the flexibility to enable us to hit rogue balls during racquet sports, and the fine control to make tasks like painting possible. From typing to holding a coffee cup, functional wrists are essential to normal everyday life. But they are easily damaged, and we all need to start thinking about them earlier in life than you’d expect. Here's how to protect yours, so you can continue taking them for granted for years to come. We may think of the wrist as a single joint, but it is actually a complex , comprising multiple smaller joints. These are formed of eight small bones known as the carpal bones, the two long bones of the forearm, and the bases of the five metacarpal bones within the palm.  "Every ligament and every bone in the wrist that connects it to your forearm bones are really in a very finely-tuned balance," says Andrew Abadeer, an assistant professor at the University of South Florida. "When that goes awry, that's when wrist arthritis starts to develop." Injuries , combined with the effects of ageing , can disrupt this fragile equilibrium. Simply avoiding arthritis is a major reason for maintaining your wrist health. There are many different kinds, but it typically takes one of three forms: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. The latter two ailments occur when the cartilage cushioning the small bones within the wrist becomes damaged, or the bones become misaligned. Both are linked to the long-term effects of injuries to the ligaments and bones within the wrist, or lingering inflammation due to overuse through repetitive manual tasks.  Sara Larsson, a researcher who studies wrist rehabilitation at Lund University, explains that this trauma may be as simple as a repetitive twisting movement or tripping and falling on an outstretched hand. "I see many people who had an injury when they were young, everything appeared to be fine again, and then 20 years later, they develop problems." Arthritis of the wrist has been estimated to affect as many as one in seven Americans . It is not only highly painful, but makes it harder for people to dress themselves and cut their own food, with the psychological burden being linked to depression. Abadeer describes the wrist as being a "sentinel joint" which can reflect early signs of declining health within the rest of the body. About half of all patients who develop rheumatoid arthritis first feel the effects the disease in their wrist before it progresses to other joints. Because the brain devotes a large region of the cortex, known as the cortical homunculus, to mapping the hands, wrist and fingers, grip strength can reflect brain structure and cognitive health. But people who reach their sixties with their wrists in better shape – typically assessed in the form of grip strength – tend to have better health overall. Those people are not only less frail and less vulnerable to falls, bone fractures and osteoporosis – a condition that weakens bones. But they are less likely to lose their independence in older age.   Before we get started, Jaehon Kim, an orthopaedic surgeon at the Ichan School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, recommends considering your diet. Foods high in calcium and other minerals, such as small, bony fish (sardines work well for this) and dairy products can help to mitigate against the development of osteoporosis. In addition, while weight might not seem particularly related to wrist health, shedding excess body fat can improve the overall biomechanics of the wrist joint. But overall, Larsson says that the best preventative measure is to do a few simple home-based workouts which can help make your wrist more resilient and stave off problems further down the line. For each of the below exercises, she recommends performing three sets of 10 repetitions (this means performing the exercise 10 times, resting, performing it again 10 times, resting, and doing it another 10 times), three or four times per week.  If you have any pre-existing conditions or injuries, it's important to seek medical advice before starting a new exercise regime. And if you feel pain at any point, stop and seek medical help.  The main muscles in your shoulders are known as the deltoids. While they may appear unrelated to wrists, Larsson says that strengthening the muscle groups across the whole arm can greatly benefit your wrist as they work together like a chain. "You don't just use your hand, you use the whole arm," says Larsson. "And if you're weak in your shoulders, then you put more load on the wrist. But if you are strong, then you can protect and unload the wrist." One easy method of training your shoulder muscles is simply to stand with your arms out to the sides, with your arms either straight or slightly bent. Slowly raise your arms up to the ceiling and then bring them down again slowly. Repeat this ten times. Grip strengthening exercises can improve wrist stability by conditioning groups of forearm muscles known as flexors and extensors, which attach to your fingers across the wrist joint, allowing you to grip objects. Studies have previously shown that this can also help people with existing wrist pain.  "All your forearm muscles connect into your hand on both sides of your wrist in a pulley system," says Abadeer. To work these muscles, you ideally want a hand therapy ball or therapeutic putty – a silicone-based material which you can squeeze in your hand – but a tennis ball will do. Hold the ball or putty in the palm of your hand and squeeze it as hard as you can for five to 10 seconds. Release the grip and relax your hand for another five seconds and then squeeze again. Repeat ten times in each hand. (Read more from the BBC about how grip strength can predict your chances of living to 100 .) According to Kim, another key means of reducing the stress on the wrist joints and tendons is exercises that flex and extend the wrist, using some form of mild weight or resistance as a load. This can also strengthen bones in the wrist, which could have longer-term health benefits, particularly when it comes to preventing a type of osteoporosis known as disuse osteopenia. "When they're loaded, these bones strengthen and start to remodel, adding more strength to the wall of that bone," says Abadeer. To do this, start by sitting and resting your forearm on a table with your hand hanging off the edge and holding a small weight, between 3 and 7kg (5 and 15lb). For a flexion exercise, have your palm facing upwards and curl your wrist up toward your body before lowering it back down again. For an extension exercise, have your palm facing downwards while holding the weight, and lift your hand up towards the ceiling before lowering it down again.  If you don't have weights, Larsson suggests using a resistance band instead. Fix one end of the band under a table leg and hold the other end across your wrist so you're experiencing some resistance while carrying out the exercises. Repeat both flexion and extension ten times. "I think this can go a long way in terms of helping the joints in your wrist, especially if you're typing and writing a lot," says Kim.   Lastly, there are supination and pronation movements. These can improve the range of motion of your wrist and its overall functionality. Like the flexion and extension exercises, they can be carried out over a table with a small weight or resistance band. Begin with your hand over the edge of the table with your thumb pointing up. Then slowly turn your wrist so your palm faces down, then return to the starting position, and rotate the other way so your palm faces up. Repeat this ten times. More like this: •  How to future-proof your hearing •  How to future-proof your brain for the 21st Century •  How to future-proof your knees   Abadeer says that such exercises are becoming increasingly important as we now live in what he describes as "a pronated world", where our hands spend many hours of the day in a fixed position, either due to typing on a laptop or a phone.  As with all our joints, strong, flexible wrists are something that we often take for granted. But as I found myself when my wrist was out of action for many months, it's only when you lose something that you realise its true importance. *  All content within this article is provided for general information only, and should not be treated as a substitute for the medical advice of health care professionals. **A previous version of this article included an incorrect figure for the heaviest weight ever lifted. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Health Human body Science Features

16小时前 分享 保存 在Google上设为偏好 David Cox 现代生活正在毁掉我们的手腕。我们都能为此做点什么，但尽早开始会更有帮助。一切始于隐隐作痛。在一个夏天的时间里，它迅速恶化为一种令手臂颤抖的剧痛，每当我击打网球或甚至试图开门时，疼痛便从左手中辐射而出。那时我18岁，打竞技网球是我生活中的重要部分，但我刚刚经历了一次将困扰我多年的伤病。如今，近二十年过去，它可能增加我患上手腕关节炎的风险。这类问题在中年及以后的生活中出奇地普遍。

##段落 我们的手腕具有惊人的适应能力。它们拥有让我们举起重物（包括2,422公斤（5339磅）的世界纪录）的力量，具备在球拍运动中击打刁钻球的灵活性，以及使绘画等任务成为可能的精细控制力。从打字到握咖啡杯，功能健全的手腕对日常生活的正常运转至关重要。但它们很容易受损，而且我们都需要在比预期更早的人生阶段开始关注它们。以下是如何保护你的手腕，以便你能在未来的岁月里继续视其为理所当然。

##段落 我们可能将手腕视为一个单一关节，但它实际上是一个复杂的结构，由多个较小的关节组成。这些关节由八块被称为腕骨的小骨、前臂的两根长骨以及手掌内五块掌骨的基底部构成。“手腕中每一根韧带和每一块连接前臂骨骼的骨头，都处于一种非常精妙的平衡状态，”南佛罗里达大学助理教授Andrew Abadeer说。“当这种平衡被打破时，手腕关节炎就开始发展了。”损伤加上衰老的影响，会破坏这种脆弱的平衡。

##段落 仅仅避免关节炎就是维持手腕健康的一个主要原因。关节炎有许多不同类型，但通常表现为三种形式之一：类风湿性关节炎、骨关节炎或创伤后关节炎。后两种疾病发生在手腕内小骨之间的软骨缓冲受损或骨骼错位时。两者都与手腕内韧带和骨骼损伤的长期影响有关，或因重复性体力劳动过度使用而导致的持续炎症有关。隆德大学研究手腕康复的研究员Sara Larsson解释说，这种创伤可能简单到如重复扭转动作或绊倒时用手撑地。“我看到许多人在年轻时受过伤，一切似乎又恢复正常，但二十年后，他们开始出现问题。”手腕关节炎已被证实与这些因素密切相关。

据估计，多达七分之一的美国人受到影响。这不仅极其痛苦，还使人们更难自己穿衣和切食物，其心理负担与抑郁症有关。阿巴迪尔将手腕描述为一个“哨兵关节”，可以反映身体其他部位健康状况恶化的早期迹象。大约一半的类风湿性关节炎患者首先在手腕上感受到疾病的影响，然后才发展到其他关节。由于大脑将一大片皮层区域（称为皮层侏儒）用于映射手、手腕和手指，握力可以反映大脑结构和认知健康。但那些年过六十、手腕状况更好——通常以握力形式评估——的人，往往整体健康状况更佳。他们不仅不那么脆弱，也不那么容易跌倒、骨折和患上骨质疏松症——一种削弱骨骼的疾病。而且他们在老年时期失去独立性的可能性也更小。在我们开始之前，纽约西奈山伊坎医学院的骨科外科医生杰洪·金建议考虑你的饮食。富含钙和其他矿物质的食物，如小鱼带骨鱼（沙丁鱼对此很有效）和乳制品，有助于缓解骨质疏松症的发展。此外，虽然体重看起来与手腕健康关系不大，但减掉多余体脂可以改善手腕关节的整体生物力学。但总体而言，拉尔森表示，最好的预防措施是做一些简单的居家锻炼，这可以帮助你的手腕更具韧性，并避免日后出现更多问题。对于以下每项练习，她建议每次进行三组，每组10次重复（这意味着执行练习10次，休息，再执行10次，休息，再做10次），每周三到四次。如果你已有任何现有疾病或损伤，在开始新的锻炼计划前务必寻求医疗建议。如果在任何时候感到疼痛，请停止并寻求医疗帮助。你肩膀的主要肌肉被称为三角肌。虽然它们看起来与手腕无关，但拉尔森表示，加强整个手臂的肌肉群可以大大有益于你的手腕，因为它们像链条一样协同工作。“你不仅仅使用手，你使用整个手臂，”拉尔森说。“如果你的肩膀力量弱，那么手腕就会承受更多负荷。但如果你强壮，那么你可以保护并减轻手腕的负担。”一种锻炼肩部肌肉的简单方法是站立，双臂向两侧伸展，手臂可以伸直或略微弯曲。慢慢抬起你的……

双臂向上举至天花板，然后缓慢放下。重复十次。握力强化练习可以通过锻炼前臂肌群（即屈肌和伸肌）来改善手腕稳定性，这些肌肉通过腕关节附着在手指上，使你能够抓握物体。先前的研究表明，这也有助于缓解已有的手腕疼痛。“你所有的前臂肌肉通过腕关节两侧的滑轮系统连接到手部，”阿巴迪尔说。要锻炼这些肌肉，理想情况下你需要一个手部治疗球或治疗性腻子——一种可以握在手中挤压的硅基材料——但网球也可以。将球或腻子放在手掌中，尽可能用力挤压五到十秒。松开握力，放松手部五秒，然后再次挤压。每只手重复十次。（从BBC了解更多关于握力如何预测你活到100岁的几率。）据金姆介绍，减轻腕关节和肌腱压力的另一个关键方法是进行手腕屈伸练习，使用某种轻度重量或阻力作为负荷。这还可以增强手腕骨骼，可能带来长期的健康益处，尤其是在预防一种被称为废用性骨量减少的骨质疏松症方面。“当这些骨骼受到负荷时，它们会增强并开始重塑，增加骨骼壁的强度，”阿巴迪尔说。要进行这项练习，先坐下，将前臂放在桌子上，手悬在边缘外，握住一个小重量，约3至7公斤（5至15磅）。对于屈曲练习，手掌朝上，将手腕向上卷向身体，然后放下。对于伸展练习，手掌朝下握住重量，将手向上举向天花板，然后放下。如果没有重量，拉尔森建议使用阻力带代替。将带子的一端固定在桌腿下，另一端横跨手腕握住，这样在练习时会感受到一些阻力。重复屈曲和伸展各十次。“我认为这对帮助手腕关节大有裨益，尤其是如果你经常打字和写字，”金姆说。最后是旋后和旋前动作。这些动作可以改善手腕的活动范围和整体功能。与屈伸练习类似，可以在桌子上用小重量或阻力带进行。开始时，手悬在桌子边缘外，拇指朝上。然后慢慢转动手腕，使手掌朝下，返回起始位置，然后向另一方向旋转。

将手掌朝上。重复这个动作十次。更多类似内容：• 如何为你的听力做好未来防护 • 如何为你的大脑做好21世纪的未来防护 • 如何为你的膝盖做好未来防护  
阿巴迪尔表示，这类锻炼正变得越来越重要，因为我们如今生活在一个他称之为“旋前世界”的环境中，双手每天有许多小时都处于固定姿势，无论是打字使用笔记本电脑还是手机。  
与所有关节一样，强壮且灵活的手腕常常被我们视为理所当然。但正如我亲身经历的那样，当我的手腕数月无法活动时，我才意识到，只有失去某样东西时，你才会真正体会到它的重要性。  
* 本文所有内容仅供一般信息参考，不应被视为替代医疗保健专业人士建议的用途。  
**本文的先前版本曾包含一个关于举重最重纪录的错误数字。  
——如需获取值得信赖的健康与福祉见解，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》新闻通讯，她还开设了《活得更久更好》与《平静六步法》课程。

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

##段落
感觉被老板忽视？你可以这样做  
2023年6月15日  
/  
海莉·考德威尔  
Facebook  
X  
LinkedIn  
Reddit  
WhatsApp  
Stocksy  

##段落
你是否曾经有过这样的经历：你的努力工作——包括你的成功——被经理视而不见？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而生——帮助那些带着职场烦恼来电的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西丝·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了来电者奈阿。在一次重大重组后，她与一位忙碌的新老板搭档，一直难以获得认可。奈阿尽心尽力地把工作做好，但缺乏对她工作的认可、鼓励——甚至关注——让她逐渐失去动力。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情的人性面——也看清你经理的人性面。

##段落
“有时候，阻碍你与经理成为优秀合作伙伴的，可能是对现状仍存有的一些残余挫败感，”安妮解释道。“但那种情绪对你不会有帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿认识到经理的人性，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮还分享了这样一个策略供她练习：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西丝是这样说的：“你在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。所以如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼多份兼职的人时，我们该如何帮助他们走向成功？”

##段落
“好奇心——在工作场所中真正神奇的灵丹妙药——最简单的表达形式就是提问，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问经理，用什么方式让他们了解你的成就和贡献最有效。或者，你也可以专注于如何让你们的会面更高效，问问他们：“我们的一对一交流如何能为我们共同要实现的目标服务？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚表达你的担忧，并询问经理他们对你成功的愿景是什么样子的。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我非常努力地工作，在这种变动不定的状态下，我担心六个月过去了，人们会怀疑我是否把工作做好了。所以对我来说，明确‘什么才算做好工作，以及我如何帮你获得这些信息？’会很有帮助。”

##段落
跨行业、跨地域，许多人都正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，需要经历一段重新调整期，这都是正常的。

从提问开始——把老板视为与你合作的普通人——可以帮助你重新获得一些主动权与自主性。  
“试着做你能做的，然后惊叹于对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一张你希望对方如何改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我认为你会惊喜地发现；这正是这件事的美好之处。”  
无论你从事何种工作或经营何种业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到可操作的建议，改善你的工作日。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩展你的副业项目，以及主持更有成效的会议。另外：点击此处，有机会在节目中让你的工作问题得到解答！现在就在你获取播客的任何平台收听《Fixable》。
