readings.title: Is New York's cannabis business flying high?
body: 26 March 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Mike Wendling Five years after it was legalised in the state, cannabis is seemingly everywhere in New York. But, business owners say that many legitimate outlets are struggling – largely because of a thriving grey market, and the complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry. If you've recently visited New York, you've probably noticed something.  Advertisements outside bodegas display pictures of bright green flowers, higher-end dispensaries that resemble coffee bars or electronics shops welcome customers from all over the world, and then of course there's the smell – so seemingly omnipresent that even US Open tennis players have complained .  Weed is everywhere. From the outside it looks like a free-for-all, one that is drawing scepticism even from voices broadly supportive of the aims of the legalisation – including reducing harm and boosting tax revenue. Social media is rife with complaints (typical comments include "New York could not have screwed up legal weed any worse!") and for years the local press has been chronicling the rise of the "weed bodega" – typically a corner store selling products of dubious provenance. Across the country, weed consumption has increased – though studies indicate  that the rate of young people using has gradually declined since the turn of the century.  Things may have come to a head recently when the  New York Times , once a legal weed supporter, published an editorial headlined: "Marijuana Is Everywhere. That's a Problem." The newspaper now argues that "marijuana is causing more harm than predicted" and calls for tighter regulation.  But this new green rush is not as straightforward as it seems. Business owners say that public perceptions have been sullied by illegal operators, and that many above-board businesses are struggling – largely because of the incredibly complicated legal status of the US cannabis industry.  "At first glance, New York's cannabis industry appears to be booming," says Jayson Tantalo, a cannabis businessman and vice president of operations for the New York Cannabis Retail Association. "But that perception was initially driven by an oversaturation of illicit operators.  "These shops often presented themselves as legitimate, creating a misleading sense of scale and economic success," he says.  New York state legalised recreational use of cannabis five years ago this month . But legal wrangling and slow issuing of licenses hampered initial growth, while sales in other states such as California were racing ahead.   The bottleneck was so restrictive that some growers in New York complained that their crops were going to waste because of the lack of retail sales outlets. Meanwhile hundreds of those shady outlets sprang up, particularly in New York City.  Those wild days may be coming to an end. State authorities are starting to crack down on illegal operators, and police have been given power to immediately shut shops without a licence. And more legal businesses are being set up to address pent-up demand.  "It was really out of control," says Vlad Bautista, co-founder of Happy Munkey, a cannabis retailer in the Inwood neighbourhood of Manhattan.  "It made a little dent," he says of recent enforcement efforts. "But there’s still a long way to go." CRB Monitor, a firm that researches the cannabis industry, counts more than 2,000 active cannabis business licenses across the state – including retailers, wholesalers, growers and other types of cannabis companies – with another nearly 5,000 applications in the pipeline.  The effects can be seen far from Manhattan with weed shops popping up all across a state that is roughly the size of England.  Jayson Tantalo owns one of them. He was involved in the weed business long before it was legal. "What started as survival evolved into deep expertise in the industry," he says. He and his wife Britni set up their Flower City Dispensary retail business in Victor, a suburban community in western New York state with a population of about 16,000.  Tantalo says that while the industry is "highly visible and normalised" across the state, only a small percentage of legal operators have captured large shares of the market.  "Growth exists, but it's constrained, uneven, and still stabilising," he says.  New York's growing pains are just one example of the extraordinarily complicated legal status of cannabis that has caused confusion across the country - for businesses, customers and the public.  The patchwork legal regime around the industry is a product of cannabis's long strange trip from respectability to contraband and back again. George Washington, the first US president, famously grew hemp crops at his estate.   But waves of restrictions followed, culminating in a 1970 law that deemed marijuana a Schedule I drug – the most restrictive category.  Despite the US government's war on drugs, there has always been a significant movement calling for looser regulations on cannabis. That movement gradually became more mainstream in the early years of this century.  Support for legalising cannabis first cracked 50% of Americans in 2013, according to polling firm Gallup, and that figure has since risen to more than two-thirds today.  But instead of blanket legalisation, reforms came in piecemeal fashion, on the state and sometimes even the local level, creating a fragmented state-by-state market.  To top it off, weed remains illegal under federal law – thousands of people still get arrested each year for marijuana possession and related crimes.  This legal patchwork results in some bizarre consequences. A road-tripper heading west from New York would pass through Pennsylvania, where recreational use of marijuana is illegal, and then into Ohio, where it was legalised by a 2023 referendum. If they continued along Interstate 80 they would eventually get to Indiana (where weed is illegal), Illinois (legal), and Iowa (illegal) – and so on.  That's confusing in itself. But another legal loophole has opened the door for all sorts of grey-market and online businesses, effectively making cannabis accessible to nearly everyone in the country.  The 2018 Farm Bill legalised hemp with a relatively low level of tetrahydrocannabinol or THC – the chemical that gets cannabis users high.  Hemp contains CBD – a chemical that doesn’t produce the high of THC but has some health benefits. A glut of CBD ensued. And in a lab, CBD can be converted into psychoactive THC.  "Entrepreneurs could say, 'this is just hemp', even if what they were producing was a highly intoxicating form of THC," says Chris Lindsay, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp (ATACH), which represents licenced businesses.  Those products are sold online or in those weed bodegas – even in states that have not legalised marijuana.  Robin Goldstein, an economist at the University of California-Davis and co-author of the book Can Legal Weed Win?: The Blunt Realities of Cannabis Economics, estimates that just behind California, the second-biggest weed market is in Texas, despite the Lone Star state's blanket ban on recreational cannabis use.  Business owners like Jason Ambrosino, have become used to dealing with spiralling legal complexities.  Ambrosino is founder and chief executive of Veterans Holdings, a weed business based in Gloversville, New York, about three hours north of New York City. An army vet who was seriously injured in Iraq, he got into the cannabis industry after discovering that medical marijuana was effective in alleviating his pain. These days, he says his legal headaches include rules that make it impossible to branch out into neighbouring states or to obtain traditional sources of financing.  "There’s a million different ways to get institutional funding, but you can’t get any of those for cannabis because of federal law," he says.  Despite the headwinds, Ambrosino has managed to grow his business and now employs around 80 people, and is hopeful that the increased licences for legal shops in New York will mean more sales opportunities down the line.  Vlad Bautista, the Happy Munkey co-founder, roughly estimates that he spends 40% of his time complying with various regulations, and, in particular, he questions some of the rules around advertising and tax law.  "If you own a cannabis business, you have much stricter advertising regulations than companies selling alcohol, cigarettes or gambling," he says. "You're stuck in the stone age, handing out flyers on the street." A buzz ran through the industry in December of last year, when President Trump signed an executive order which directed officials to accelerate efforts to reclassify marijuana to a less stringent category.  That might eventually give cannabis businesses some added profits – due to another federal law, weed companies aren't able to deduct all of their normal business expenses from their taxes. But businesspeople and experts aren't holding their breath for a practical impact any time soon.  "It's smoke and mirrors," says Naomi Granger, founder and chief executive of the National Association of Cannabis Accounting and Tax Professionals, who says some headlines heralding a new dawn for the cannabis industry have been somewhat misleading.  Some industry insiders say uncertainty is part and parcel of a nascent industry.  Steve Kemmerling, founder and chief executive of CRB Monitor, notes that states that were earlier to legal weed – California and Colorado in the western US were among the first – experienced hiccups on the way to relative stability.  "In any new market you're going to have wild volatility and price swings, mergers and acquisitions, along with competitive businesses and people cutting corners," he says.  And in a buzzy industry perhaps it's not surprising to encounter businesspeople who seem hard wired for sunny-day thinking.  "I'm an optimist," says Vlad Bautista. "We live in a divided and polarised world where nobody agrees on everything, and when you look at public opinion, there's a majority of people who agree on legal cannabis." "We've made a ton of progress," he says, "but there's still a long way to go." 在纽约州合法化五年后，大麻似乎无处不在。但企业主表示，许多合法门店正举步维艰——主要归因于蓬勃发展的灰色市场，以及美国大麻产业复杂的法律地位。

如果你最近去过纽约，你可能会注意到一些现象。杂货店外的广告展示着亮绿色花朵的图片，高端药房形似咖啡吧或电子产品店，欢迎着来自世界各地的顾客，当然还有那气味——似乎无处不在，连美国网球公开赛的选手都抱怨过。大麻无处不在。

从表面看，这像是一场无序竞争，甚至引来了一些原本支持合法化目标（包括减少危害和增加税收）的声音的质疑。社交媒体上充斥着抱怨（典型评论如“纽约不可能把合法大麻搞得更糟了！”），多年来当地媒体一直在报道“大麻杂货店”的兴起——这类店铺通常销售来源可疑的产品。全美范围内，大麻消费量有所增加——尽管研究表明，自世纪之交以来，年轻人的使用率已逐渐下降。

事情最近可能达到了顶点，《纽约时报》——曾是合法大麻的支持者——发表了一篇题为“大麻无处不在。这是个问题。”的社论。该报现在认为“大麻造成的危害比预期的更大”，并呼吁加强监管。

但这场新的绿色热潮并不像表面看起来那么简单。企业主表示，公众看法已被非法经营者玷污，许多合法企业正面临困境——主要归因于美国大麻产业极其复杂的法律地位。

“乍一看，纽约的大麻产业似乎在蓬勃发展，”大麻商人兼纽约大麻零售协会运营副总裁Jayson Tantalo说。“但这种看法最初是由非法经营者的过度饱和所推动的。”

“这些店铺往往伪装成合法经营，制造了一种关于规模和经济效益的误导性印象，”他说。

纽约州在本月迎来了娱乐用大麻合法化五周年。但法律纠纷和许可证发放缓慢阻碍了初期增长，而加利福尼亚等其他州的销售却在飞速发展。这一瓶颈如此严格，以至于一些纽约种植者抱怨，由于缺乏零售销售渠道，他们的作物正在浪费。与此同时，数百家那些可疑店铺如雨后春笋般涌现，尤其是在

在纽约市，那些狂野的日子可能即将结束。州当局开始打击非法经营者，警方已被授权立即关闭无照商店。同时，更多合法企业正在设立，以满足被压抑的需求。“当时真的失控了，”曼哈顿因伍德区大麻零售商Happy Munkey的联合创始人弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。谈到近期的执法行动，他表示“这起了一点作用，但还有很长的路要走。”研究大麻行业的公司CRB Monitor统计，全州有超过2000个活跃的大麻商业许可证——包括零售商、批发商、种植者及其他类型的大麻公司——另有近5000份申请正在审批中。这种影响远远超出了曼哈顿，在这个面积大致相当于英格兰的州内，大麻商店遍地开花。杰森·坦塔洛就是其中一位店主。他在大麻合法化之前很久就涉足这一行业。“最初是为了生存，后来演变成对行业的深入了解，”他说。他和妻子布里特尼在纽约州西部维克多郊区社区（人口约16000）开设了他们的Flower City Dispensary零售店。坦塔洛表示，尽管该行业在全州“高度可见且已常态化”，但只有少数合法经营者占据了较大市场份额。“增长存在，但受到限制、不均衡，且仍在稳定过程中，”他说。纽约的成长阵痛只是大麻极其复杂法律地位的一个例子，这种状况已在全美范围内给企业、消费者和公众造成困惑。围绕该行业的零散法律体系，源于大麻从体面到违禁品再回归的漫长奇异旅程。美国第一任总统乔治·华盛顿以在其庄园种植大麻而闻名。但随后一波波限制接踵而至，最终在1970年的一项法律中，大麻被列为第一类管制药物——即最严格的类别。尽管美国政府发起禁毒战争，但一直有重要运动呼吁放宽对大麻的管制。本世纪初，这场运动逐渐走向主流。根据民调公司盖洛普的数据，2013年，支持大麻合法化的美国人比例首次突破50%，而如今这一数字已升至三分之二以上。但改革并非全面合法化，而是在州甚至地方层面零敲碎打地推进，形成了各州各自为政的碎片化市场。更糟的是，大麻在联邦法律下仍属非法——每年仍有数千人因持有大麻及相关犯罪被捕。这种法律拼凑局面……

法律工作的结果有时会引发一些奇怪的现象。一名从纽约向西出发的公路旅行者会穿过宾夕法尼亚州，在那里娱乐用大麻是非法的，然后进入俄亥俄州，那里在2023年的公投中将其合法化。如果他们继续沿80号州际公路行驶，最终会到达印第安纳州（大麻非法）、伊利诺伊州（合法）和爱荷华州（非法），如此反复。这本身就令人困惑。但另一个法律漏洞为各种灰色市场和在线业务打开了大门，实际上使美国几乎所有人都能接触到这种物质。

2018年的农业法案将四氢大麻酚（THC）含量相对较低的大麻合法化，THC是让大麻使用者产生兴奋感的化学物质。大麻含有CBD——一种不会产生THC那种兴奋感但具有某些健康益处的化学物质。随后CBD出现了过剩。而在实验室中，CBD可以转化为具有精神活性的THC。美国大麻和大麻贸易协会（ATACH）的政策和州宣传副总裁克里斯·林赛表示：“企业家们可以说‘这只是大麻’，即使他们生产的是高度致醉形式的THC。”ATACH代表持牌企业。这些产品在网上或在那些大麻杂货店出售，即使在未将大麻合法化的州也是如此。

加州大学戴维斯分校的经济学家、《合法大麻能赢吗？：大麻经济的直率现实》一书的合著者罗宾·戈德斯坦估计，仅次于加利福尼亚州，第二大大麻市场是德克萨斯州，尽管孤星州全面禁止娱乐用大麻。像杰森·安布罗西诺这样的企业主已经习惯于应对日益复杂的法律问题。安布罗西诺是总部位于纽约州格洛弗斯维尔的大麻企业Veterans Holdings的创始人兼首席执行官，该地距离纽约市以北约三小时车程。他是一名在伊拉克严重受伤的退伍军人，在发现医用大麻能有效缓解他的疼痛后进入了这一行业。如今，他说他的法律头疼问题包括一些规则，这些规则使他无法扩展到邻近州或获得传统的融资来源。

他说：“有无数种方式可以获得机构资金，但由于联邦法律，你无法为大麻获得任何一种。”尽管面临这些逆风，安布罗西诺还是成功发展了他的业务，现在雇佣了大约80名员工，并对纽约合法商店牌照的增加将意味着未来更多销售机会抱有希望。Happy Munkey联合创始人弗拉德·巴蒂斯塔粗略估计，他花费40%的时间来遵守各种法规，特别是质疑一些关于广告和税法的规则。“如果你拥有一家大麻……”

他指出：“相比销售酒类、香烟或赌博产品的公司，你的广告监管要严格得多。你就像困在石器时代，只能在街上发传单。”去年十二月，特朗普总统签署了一项行政命令，指示官员加速将大麻重新归类到更宽松的类别，这在整个行业引起了轰动。这最终可能为大麻企业带来额外利润——因为根据另一项联邦法律，大麻公司无法从税收中扣除所有正常业务开支。但商界人士和专家并未急于期待近期内产生实际影响。全国大麻会计与税务专业人士协会的创始人兼首席执行官娜奥米·格兰杰表示：“这不过是烟雾弹。”她认为，一些预示大麻行业新纪元的头条新闻有些误导性。一些业内人士表示，不确定性是新行业的固有特征。CRB Monitor的创始人兼首席执行官史蒂夫·凯默林指出，较早合法化大麻的州——美国西部的加利福尼亚和科罗拉多是首批之一——在走向相对稳定的过程中经历了波折。他说：“在任何新市场中，你都会遇到剧烈的波动和价格震荡、并购活动，以及竞争激烈的企业和偷工减料的行为。”在这个喧嚣的行业中，遇到似乎天生乐观的企业家或许并不奇怪。“我是个乐观主义者，”弗拉德·包蒂斯塔说。“我们生活在一个分裂和两极分化的世界里，没有人能在所有事情上达成一致，但当你观察公众舆论时，大多数人同意大麻合法化。”“我们已经取得了很大进展，”他说，“但前路依然漫长。”如需药物成瘾支持，请访问BBC Action Line。——如需全球洞察和专家分析，供董事会及其他领域使用，请订阅《商业世界》通讯，而《基本清单》则提供精选特写和见解。欲了解更多商业及更多内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业毒品特写

readings.title: My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
body: Advice My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something. ﻿To save the humanities, we need to rethink our assumptions about AI — and education. by Sigal Samuel Updated Sep 6, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift Pete Gamlen for Vox Part Of The rapid development of AI has benefits — and poses serious risks see all updates Sigal Samuel is a correspondent for Vox’s Future Perfect. She writes primarily about the future of consciousness, tracking advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience and their staggering ethical implications. Before joining Vox, Sigal was the religion editor at the Atlantic. Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year. This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here . I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes. This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too. Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting. But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies. And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment. I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does. How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent? Dear Troubled Teacher, I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed! So: What is the real value of a humanities education? Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields. Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films. But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion. That’s never what they were supposed to be. Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes , is “the formation of human persons.” In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product. She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process. Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here! This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece. He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life. But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision. And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham. As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him , “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision. The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character. I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!” It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects. But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now. Your job is to be their Aristotle. For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis , or practical wisdom. And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI. Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot . It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you. Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie !). If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context. This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world. The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to. The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice. Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction . Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout. Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use. “Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it. And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.” So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing. If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy. Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit. Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without. Both are totally fine. But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process. I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using. As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it. Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it). All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have. So use every bit of it. Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation. You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite. If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them. But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion. At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim. None of this is easy. I feel for you and all other educators who are struggling in this confusing environment. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if some educators are suffering from moral injury , a psychological condition that arises when you feel you’ve been forced to violate your own values. But maybe it can comfort you to remember that this is much bigger than you. Generative AI is an existential threat to a humanities education as currently constituted. Over the next few years, humanities departments will have to paradigm-shift or perish. If they want to survive, they’ll need to get brutally honest about their true mission. For now, from your pre-paradigm-shift perch, all you can do is make the choices that are left for you to make. I went back to Shannon Vallor’s first book, Technology and the Virtues: A Philosophical Guide to a Future Worth Wanting . If there’s one book I could get everyone in the AI world to read, it would be this one. And I think it can be useful to everyone else, too, because we all need to cultivate what Vallor calls the “technomoral virtues” — the traits that will allow us to adapt well to emerging technologies. A New Yorker piece about AI and cognitive atrophy led me to a 2024 psychology paper titled “The Unpleasantness of Thinking: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Association Between Mental Effort and Negative Affect.” The authors’ conclusion: “We suggest that mental effort is inherently aversive.” Come again? Yes, sometimes I just want to turn off my brain and watch Netflix, but sometimes thinking about a challenging topic is so pleasurable! To me, it feels like running or weightlifting: Too much is exhausting, but the right amount is exhilarating. And what feels like “the right amount” can go up or down depending on how much I practice. Astrobiologist Sara Imari Walker published an essay in Noema provocatively titled “ AI Is Life .” She reminds us that evolution produced us and we produced AI. “It is therefore part of the same ancient lineage of information that emerged with the origin of life,” she writes. “Technology is not artificially replacing life — it is life.” To be clear, she’s not arguing that tech is alive; she’s saying it’s an outgrowth of human life, an extension of our own species. This story was originally published in The Highlight , Vox’s member-exclusive magazine. To get early access to member-exclusive stories every month, join the Vox Membership program today . By Sigal Samuel A guide to finding meaning at work in the age of AI By Sigal Samuel The one question everyone should be asking after OpenAI’s deal with the Pentagon By Sigal Samuel Take a mental break with the newest Vox crossword The biggest advocate for slaughtering America’s wild horses might surprise you An evangelical explains what people get wrong about her faith Gen Z’s politics aren’t what people think Podcast A guy made a deepfake app to turn photos of women into nudes. 我的学生们认为用AI作弊没问题。也许他们发现了什么。为了拯救人文学科，我们需要重新思考对AI——以及教育——的假设。作者：西格尔·塞缪尔 更新于2026年9月6日，UTC时间中午12:00 礼物 皮特·甘伦为Vox绘制 部分 AI的快速发展带来了好处——也带来了严重风险 查看所有更新 西格尔·塞缪尔是Vox“未来完美”栏目的记者。她主要撰写关于意识未来的文章，追踪人工智能和神经科学的进展及其令人震惊的伦理影响。加入Vox之前，西格尔是《大西洋月刊》的宗教编辑。编者按，9月6日东部时间上午8点：在西格尔·塞缪尔休产假期间，我们为您带来一些最受欢迎的“里程可能因人而异”专栏。以下这篇最初发表于去年。这期非传统建议专栏为您提供了一个独特的框架，用来思考道德困境。它基于价值多元主义：即我们每个人都拥有多种价值，这些价值同样有效，但常常相互冲突。在此提交您自己的问题。我是一名大学助教，负责大型人文学科讲座课程的讨论小组。这也意味着我要批改大量学生写作——而且，不可避免地，也会看到大量AI写作。当然，我们很多人都在努力设计作业和教学法，以降低这种诱惑。但作为助教，我实施这些政策的能力有限。与此同时，AI生成的写作如此普遍，以至于要认真对待课程政策，甚至把每一个疑似案例都上报给授课教授，那基本上每份作业都要提出几十次指控，其中一些还是误报。我相信人文学科教育具有神圣不可言喻的价值，但我也不会通过对每个人都在做的事情进行严厉打压，去说服那些压力重重的19岁学生相信这种价值。我该如何思考执行一个他们并不认真对待的机构的规则的伦理问题，或者为了营造一个不那么像需要绕过的障碍的课堂而放任自流？亲爱的烦恼的老师，我知道你说你相信“人文学科教育不可言喻的价值”，但如果我们想真正理清你的困境，那种不可言喻的价值必须被言说出来！那么：人文学科教育的真正价值是什么？放眼现代大学，人们可能会认为人文学科与STEM领域并无太大不同。正如工程系或数学系通过指出其创造的产品——桥梁设计、天气预报——来证明自身存在的合理性，如今的人文学科系也通过指出其学生同样创造产品来证明自身存在的合理性：文学解读。

##段落
翻译、文化批评、短片。但说真的：是大学的新自由主义化迫使人文科学陷入那种怪异的扭曲。那从来不是它们本该有的样子。正如哲学家梅根·弗里茨所写，它们的真正目标是“人的形成”。换句话说，虽然其他院系的目的最终是创造产品，但人文教育本该不同，因为学生本身就是产品。她才是学习过程中被创造和再创造的对象。填写这份匿名表格！订阅者将比其他人都更早看到我的专栏，他们的问题也会在未来的版本中被优先处理。在此注册！

##段落
这种教育愿景——作为一种旨在个人转变的追求——正是亚里士多德在古希腊时期提出的。他认为真正的目标不是传授知识，而是培养美德：诚实、正义、勇气，以及所有那些促成丰盈人生的性格特质。但由于在我们的超资本主义社会中，丰盈被贬低，你发现自己被困在最初的愿景和如今基于产品、功利主义的愿景之间。而学生们——正确地！——感觉到生成式AI证明了人文科学的功利主义愿景是个骗局。正如一位学生对他在纽约大学的教授所说，为了证明用AI帮他做作业的合理性：“你让我从A点到B点，我为什么不用车去呢？”这是一个完全合乎逻辑的论点——只要你接受功利主义的愿景。那么，真正的解决方案是对人文科学的目的保持诚实：你的事业是帮助学生培养他们的品格。我知道，我知道：很多学生会说：“我没时间培养品格！我只需要找到工作！”他们专注于就业前景完全合理。但你的工作是专注于别的东西——一些能帮助他们在长远中丰盈的东西，即使他们现在不完全看到它的价值。你的工作就是做他们的亚里士多德。

##段落
对于这位古希腊哲学家来说，所有美德之母是phronesis，即实践智慧。而我想说，你能为学生做的最有用的事，莫过于帮助他们培养这种美德，而AI的出现使它变得更重要，而不是更不重要。实践智慧超越了对一般规则的简单了解——比如“不要撒谎”——并像某种道德机器人那样机械地应用它们。它关乎在面对生活抛给你的复杂、动态情境时知道如何做出良好判断。有时那实际上意味着违背一条经典规则（在某些情况下，你应该撒谎！）。如果你已经

当你磨练了实践智慧，你将能够辨别特定情境中具有道德意义的关键特征，并给出与该情境高度契合的回应。这正是学生们步入更广阔世界时需要擅长的思考方式。技术创新的飞速步伐意味着他们将不得不一次又一次地选择如何利用新兴技术——以及如何不去利用。他们现在能获得的最佳训练，就是如何明智地做出这类选择。不幸的是，课堂上使用生成式AI恰恰可能会破坏这一点，因为它移除了一种极其宝贵的东西：摩擦。遭遇摩擦是我们锻炼认知肌肉的方式。将其从画面中移除，短期内会让事情变得更容易，但从长远来看，可能导致智力上的技能退化，我们的认知肌肉因缺乏使用而逐渐减弱。“实践智慧就像其他所有美德一样，通过实践来积累，所以如果你没有机会推理，也没有机会练习对某些事情进行深思，你以后就无法很好地深思，”技术哲学家香农·瓦洛去年告诉我。“我们需要大量认知锻炼来发展并保持实践智慧。有理由担心认知自动化会剥夺我们建立和保持这些认知肌肉的机会。”那么，你如何帮助学生保持并增强他们的实践智慧呢？通过尽可能多地给他们练习深思和选择的机会，将摩擦重新引入。如果我来设计课程，我不会采用严格的“禁止AI”政策。相反，我会对学生坦诚人文学科的真实益处，并解释为何盲目地利用AI作弊就是剥夺自己获得这种益处。然后，在写论文时，我会给他们两个选择：他们可以在AI帮助下写作，或者不依赖AI。两者完全可以。但如果他们确实从AI获得帮助，他们还必须写一篇课堂反思文章，解释为什么选择使用聊天机器人，以及他们认为这如何改变了他们的思维和学习过程。我会让它比原始作业更短，但比一段更长，这样迫使他们发展出他们试图避免使用的推理技能。作为助教，你可以向教授提出这个建议，但他们可能不会采纳。不幸的是，你在这里的自主权有限（除非你愿意冒险失去工作或离开它）。在这种情况下，你所能做的就是行使你确实拥有的自主权。所以，充分利用每一分。既然你带领讨论课，你处于有利位置来引导你的学生。

来锻炼他们在对话中的认知能力。你甚至可以组织一场关于AI的辩论：让一半学生为使用聊天机器人写论文辩护，另一半则反对。如果教授坚持严格的“禁止AI”政策，而你遇到明显由AI撰写的文章，你可能别无选择，只能举报。但如果某篇文章存在疑点，而学生在讨论中表现出非常深入的思考，你或许应倾向于宽容处理。至少这样你知道他们实现了最重要的目标。这一切都不容易。我对你以及所有在这个混乱环境中挣扎的教育者深表同情。事实上，如果有些教育者正遭受道德伤害——即当你感到被迫违背自身价值观时产生的心理状态——我也不会感到惊讶。但或许可以安慰你的是，记住这件事远非你一人所能左右。生成式AI对当前形式的人文学科教育构成了生存威胁。未来几年，人文学科部门必须经历范式转变，否则将消亡。如果他们想生存，就需要对自己真正的使命进行残酷的诚实审视。目前，从你处于范式转变前的视角来看，你所能做的只是做出留给你的选择。

我回想起了Shannon Vallor的第一本书《技术与美德：值得向往未来的哲学指南》。如果有一本书能让AI世界中的每个人都读到，那非它莫属。我认为它对其他人同样有益，因为我们都需培养Vallor所称的“技术道德美德”——这些特质能让我们很好地适应新兴技术。《纽约客》上一篇关于AI与认知萎缩的文章让我找到了一篇2024年的心理学论文，题为《思考的不愉快：心理努力与负面情绪关联的元分析综述》。作者的结论是：“我们建议，心理努力本质上令人厌恶。”再说一遍？是的，有时我只想关掉大脑看Netflix，但有时思考一个挑战性话题却如此愉快！对我来说，这就像跑步或举重：太多会令人疲惫，但适量则令人振奋。而“适量”的感觉会随着我的练习多少而上下波动。天体生物学家Sara Imari Walker在《Noema》杂志上发表了一篇题为《AI是生命》的文章，颇具挑衅性。她提醒我们，进化产生了我们，而我们产生了AI。“因此，它属于与生命起源同时出现的远古信息谱系的一部分，”她写道，“技术并非人为地替代生命——它就是生命。”需要明确的是，她并非主张技术是活的；她是在说技术是人类生命的延伸。

readings.title: Why you never really get over high school
body: 2 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Laurie Clarke Popularity, one of the defining fixations of adolescence, seems to be seared into our consciousness for decades after we leave school. Before I was friends with Georgia*, I was scared of her.  One incident sticks in my mind. We were 14, and my best friend at the time was throwing a party – the kind that takes place in a rented church hall and where practically the whole school year turns up. But there was one group of people that my friend had neglected to invite. Georgia and her posse strode towards us across the playground, observers turning to stare. She was a terrifying bolt of fake tan, peroxide hair extensions and luminous sportswear – what could she possibly want with the likes of us? We froze as she came to a halt.  "We're invited to your party, yeah?" Georgia demanded of my friend. "Yes, of course," my friend managed to stutter back. Satisfied, Georgia turned on her heel and marched away. Another girl nearby murmured, "You don't have to invite them if you don't want to." But we all knew that yes, yes she did. You probably have similar high school recollections – of finding yourself at the sharp end of playground politics. Maybe you have memories of your own Georgia, a popular kid who could induce fear at a glance. Maybe you were a Georgia yourself. Either way, you probably remember it well. After speaking to hundreds of people about their experiences of high school, Mitch Prinstein, a professor of psychology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in the US, found that people's memories of those who once ruled over the school corridors – the queen bees, the prom kings, the star athletes – were remarkably potent. We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through – Mitch Prinstein Even decades after leaving school, most people are able to effortlessly recall the name of the most popular kid in their year – more so than the names of teachers and other classmates, wrote Prinstein ​i​n his 2017 book Popular: The Power of Likability in a Status-Obsessed World . And it's not just the memories that stick. We might be inclined to think that the high school hierarchy becomes irrelevant once we step beyond the school gates for the last time. But it turns out that it can exert a strange and persistent hold over us.  Research shows that how popular and well-liked we were as teenagers can influence our lives for years to come in everything from how we make sense of our social interactions to the strength of our romantic relations, our life satisfaction and even our health.  It was American psychologist John Coie who changed the way researchers thought about popularity.  His now-seminal studies in the early 1980s began by asking school kids two simple questions about their classmates: Who do you like the most? Who do you like the least? In the childish handwriting scrawled across hundreds of scraps of paper, Coie would trace new insights about human social behaviour.  You might think that children would be either broadly liked or disliked by their peers. In fact, Coie and his colleagues found kids can be both liked and disliked by different students, or neither liked nor disliked. Some children were named a lot by their peers – they were highly visible, like tiny celebrities. Others were barely mentioned at all. For the first time, Coie used the kids' answers to propose five social categories. "Accepted" and "rejected" for those who were widely liked or disliked respectively. "Controversial" for those who got a high number of both "likes" and "dislikes". "Neglected" for those who were hardly mentioned either way. And "average", for kids who weren't too extreme in any one direction (though most leaned towards one of the categories). Many studies have confirmed the usefulness of these labels. They generally find that about 40% of kids are "average" and 60% fit into one of the remaining four categories.  The most liked kids tend to be seen by their peers as kind, encouraging and supportive, while "neglecteds" tend to be quiet and withdrawn. "Rejected" kids are likely to be either aggressive and to bully others, or unassertive, socially anxious and the victims of bullying themselves . "Controversials", the rarest group, split the crowd – they're typically seen as class clowns or rebels. Remarkably, Coie found that children's labels largely stayed the same when they were introduced to new peer groups. And while the initial research was on primary school kids, many studies have replicated the findings in adolescents. One found that around half of kids maintain the same label they had at primary school five years later in high school.  "I'd had such a bad experience in primary school, and I always remember my mum saying 'It'll be better when you go to high school'," says Connie*, another friend I've asked about her high school experience. "But I think once you've been bullied, or if you have something that makes you visibly different… it was like I was easy pickings."  After being targeted by bullies in the first few months of high school, for reasons including being mixed race at a predominantly white institution, Connie switched schools. At her new school however, she soon encountered a similar pattern. (Read about the powerful new ways being discovered to fight bullying .) While the labels stay the same, the social dynamics shift dramatically between primary school and high school. In primary school, the "popular" kids are simply those who are best liked – often those who are well-behaved and excel at school, because at that point, kids values typically align with their adult supervisors. At high school, that changes . Adults and everything they stand for become woefully undesirable. A conscientious over-achiever might find themselves relegated to "nerd" status, while a rowdier, more divisive kid might find their star unexpectedly in ascendance. On the phone to the one-time playground terror and my now close friend Georgia, I ask her if she considered herself popular at high school. She tells me she didn't think of herself in this way. "'Popular' makes it sound as if people like you and I don't think we were necessarily liked," she says. "Maybe it was a bit more like, infamous… loud and attention-seeking." As a young teen, Georgia embodied the "controversial" archetype. She acted out aggressively and was disruptive in class. For all those who loved her, there were probably a fair few who didn't. I tell her that people, including myself, were pretty scared of her at one point. But she's wrong about this making her ineligible for the "popular" label.  "We start paying attention to who might be getting the most attention, who might be more dominant or 'cool'," says Prinstein. "Those who start becoming more physically attractive, those who are fitting into peer norms, [like] those who dress well or are good at sports."  Engaging in "pseudomature" behaviour – actions associated with older teens or adults – is another fast track to status. Teens who drink alcohol, take drugs and engage in precocious romantic behaviour are more likely to be considered popular – at least for a time. At around age 15, this behaviour stops conferring status to the same degree.  As high schoolers begin to mature, overt status-seeking becomes less socially expedient, and "likeability" begins to reassert itself as an important determinant of social standing. But the ripple effects from these early experiences in extreme social stratification can be consequential. "The experiences that we're having as kids – whether we're well liked, whether we're popular or high status – seem to have an enduring effect on us even 40 years later," says Prinstein. "Likability and status have pretty opposite effects. Likability is good. It generally leads to all kinds of positive health, work, academic and psychological outcomes.  "High status actually leads to the opposite ." Researchers used to think of high school culture as an immature version of adult society. In the 1960s, they began to understand that this "peer culture" was something much stranger – a parallel world animated by its own quixotic fascinations and sets of codes.  Rather than a simple hierarchy, the high school social landscape features a dynamic system of cliques. The key archetypes recur across popular culture, from American Pie to The Breakfast Club : the populars, the burnouts, the rejects and the nerds.  For the first few years of high school, the boundaries between cliques tend to be rigid. "Young people can become remarkably clannish, intolerant and cruel in their exclusion of others who are 'different'," wrote German-American psychoanalyst Erik Erikson in his 1959 book , Identity and the Life Cycle. It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence – Lucy Foulkes This intolerance, Erikson contended, might be "a necessary defence" against the loss of the identity one had as a child, combined with a mystifying onslaught of hormonal changes, and the overwhelming nature of the future, with all its possibilities and choices. Adolescents help each other through this discomfort "by forming cliques and stereotyping themselves", he suggested. This self-sorting makes it easier for teenagers to navigate their social worlds, because each person's relative "category" dictates how they should be treated.   One thing that is overlooked in popular culture, however, is the large swathe of teens who don't subscribe to any particular subculture. A 1985 study found that about 45% of highschoolers defined themselves simply as "normal". While the popular kids claimed they were all about looking good and partying, self-defined "normals" said things like "I'm just a regular teen". Being "abnormal" and standing out for the wrong reasons can be socially catastrophic. Connie remembers arriving at her new school aged 13 and finding it impossible to gain a foothold on the slippery social edifice. She describes her attempts to amplify different parts of herself in search of the right clique.   "I remember trying to be friends with the nerdy girls. I remember trying to be friends with the cool girls," she says. "I'd be like, 'Oh, I'm really bookish, I do all my homework.' And then that wasn't working, so it was like, 'Oh, I wear makeup, I do my hair,' that sort of thing. I tried to fit in with the music people. I started playing the trumpet."  But it was to no avail. "I think I knew in my heart that it just wasn't working," she says. "There was nowhere for me to slot in. By the end, I was just completely ignored by everyone."  Towards the end of high school, the punishing social hierarchy relaxes a little.  In the early 1990s, researcher David Kinney carried out an ethnographic research project where he embedded himself in a high school to observe the shifting boundaries of cliques up close. He tracked former "nerds" who managed to transition to "normals".  The rigidity of early high school cliques might reflect the limited cognitive capacities of young adolescents, he noted . While young teens are increasingly able to self-reflect, many are unable to differentiate between how often they think about themselves (a lot) and how often others do.  For many of the young "nerds" Kinney spoke to, this resulted in a debilitating self-focus and paralysis in social interactions. Eventually, continued cognitive development meant that former nerds were able to feel less fearful, and to surround themselves with peers who provided positive feedback. As teens mature, the strictures of conformity begin to loosen. Popular kids might even face threats from alternative, rebellious types. Kinney's study found that in later years, the "trendies" were challenged by students with "outrageous appearance and rowdy behaviour", who "competed with them for schoolwide popularity".  Some of these subtle shifts must have been underway when, aged 15, Georgia first asked me to hang out with her, but I still remember experiencing confusion and disbelief. At that point, I was a member of a predominantly male group of stoners. Was Georgia trying to play some kind of practical joke on me? Would I be lured out only to be humiliated in some way?   Almost 20 years later, I ask Georgia why she wanted to befriend me, something I've never asked her before. I'm wondering which of my sparkling attributes might have attracted her attention – my wit, my charm? "I guess there was a weirdness that we all shared," she says hesitantly. "Like, none of us were normal."  Given all its unique quirks, it’s remarkable how often we use high school as a frame of reference for adult interactions. When Lucy Foulkes, a psychologist at the University of Oxford in the UK and author of Coming of Age: How Adolescence Shapes Us , shared a social media post about the "mean girl" effect, she was met with an outpouring of recognition. "A lot of people were saying, it's not just teenagers, I see this in the workplace… I see this with mums at the school gate," says Foulkes. "It's a human phenomenon that some people achieve more social power and dominance over others. There's just something particularly acute about it in adolescence."  Foulkes points out that teens are surrounded by the same people almost every day for years in a way "that just doesn't really happen in adulthood, other than in the army or in prison. There is an intensity from the environment that goes beyond what's happening inside their brains." It's this intensity that partly explains why these experiences stay lodged within us, says Prinstein, shaping how we make sense of social encounters for years to come.  "We're calling forth those experiences from when we were 14 to use as a kind of a template to see the world through," says Prinstein. He points to studies suggesting that the mental model we use to process our social worlds begins to form in childhood , and that the memory-processing parts of the brain are active when people think about social behaviour . "Those memories are being brought back out all the time."  Many of us have likely wondered what happened to the "cool kids" we knew as teens. In a 2015 study , Joseph Allen, a professor of psychology at the University of Virginia in the US, sought to find out. His discoveries did not bode well for once-popular youths. Following 184 adolescents in the south-eastern US from ages 13 to 23, Allen found that status-hungry young people who engaged in pseudomature behaviour in their early teens were at greater risk of long-term difficulties in close relationships and criminal behaviour.  An early taste for alcohol and drugs was tied to greater vulnerability to substance abuse and addiction issues later in life. And a focus on status at an early age led to shallower bonds and difficulties sustaining friendships and romantic relationships.  The experience of being rejected can also leave scars. Prinstein's research found that rejected high school students were likely to become more depressed over time . He hypothesised that a negative feedback loop was at play, where the experience of rejection begets more withdrawal, which in turn intensifies feelings of rejection. People can absolutely turn it around. The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – Mitch Prinstein By contrast, "likeability" – being "accepted" – in high school and generally, is one of the strongest predictors for positive life outcomes like a successful career , good health and strong relationships , even over and above factors like intelligence and socioeconomic background. Still, people who experience rejection can also develop important strengths, such as becoming more adept at identifying how others are feeling or being more aware of others being mistreated . Such emotional intelligence has been shown to be helpful in navigating personal relationships and the world of work .  And a child doesn't have to be "accepted" to enjoy a fulfilling social life as an adult. Studies have found that even just having one or two good friends as a teenager can confer a protective effect and strengthen future relationships.   Most importantly, it's within our power to change how our early experiences affect us. According to Prinstein, the high-school-honed social scripts we approach interactions with can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. "When we enter into a social context, we may be focusing on those pieces of information that confirm our worst expectations," he says. "Then we will behave in ways that might actually encourage more negative experiences." By choosing to update these frameworks – for example, deciding that a peer's ambiguous comment was probably not intended to upset us – we can help ourselves to have more rewarding experiences, he says.  As a reformed "high status" teen who engaged in risky, pseudomature behaviour from a young age, Georgia says, "I kind of have a sadness for my younger self, that I never got to experience just being a normal kid." She tells me that an early experience of seeing a friend beaten up, combined with abusive behaviour at home, convinced her to act aggressively to project invulnerability.  More like this: • The perks and pitfalls of laughing at yourself • How much of our personalities are determined at birth? • How I changed my personality in six weeks   She laments the fact that she didn't get more support at that age and was instead typecast by teachers as a "bad kid". "It's completely shaped my career trajectory and my fierce advocacy for vulnerable people," she says. Connie, meanwhile, says her early experiences of rejection eventually fed into a pattern of self-sabotage. "I think I'd given up on myself in a lot of ways, and I had so many self-destructive behaviours that it then became hard to maintain friendships," she says. This culminated in a period of crisis in her late adolescence, which she has since worked hard to heal from. More than a decade on, she has figured out what she loves – including a creative practice and a fulfilling career – and says she rarely thinks about her high school days.  Both Connie and Georgia are testament to the fact that the labels we once wore in high school don't have to be a life sentence.  "People can absolutely turn it around," Prinstein concurs. "The problem is that we don't spend a lot of time talking about this – meaning we are more likely to repeat our patterns."  * Names have been changed. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter   by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses. 2天前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 Laurie Clarke 受欢迎程度，青春期最具定义性的迷恋之一，似乎在我们离开学校几十年后仍深深烙印在意识中。在我和Georgia*成为朋友之前，我害怕她。有一件事令我印象深刻。我们当时14岁，我那时最好的朋友要办一个派对——那种在租来的教堂大厅里举行、几乎整个年级都会出席的派对。但有一群人，我的朋友忽略了邀请。Georgia和她的跟班们穿过操场向我们大步走来，旁观者纷纷转头注视。她像一道可怕的闪电，带着假晒黑、漂染的接发和荧光运动服——她可能想从我们这类人这里得到什么呢？她停下来时，我们僵住了。“我们受邀参加你的派对了，对吧？”Georgia质问我的朋友。“是的，当然，”我的朋友勉强结结巴巴地回应。满意后，Georgia转身大步走开。旁边另一个女孩低声说：“如果你不想，不必邀请她们。”但我们都知道，是的，她确实必须邀请。你可能也有类似的高中回忆——发现自己身处操场政治的风口浪尖。也许你有自己的Georgia记忆，一个一眼就能让人恐惧的受欢迎孩子。也许你自己就是Georgia。无论哪种方式，你可能都记得很清楚。在与数百人谈论他们的高中经历后，美国北卡罗来纳大学教堂山分校心理学教授Mitch Prinstein发现，人们对那些曾主宰学校走廊的人——蜂后、舞会国王、明星运动员——的记忆异常强烈。我们召唤14岁时的那些经历，作为看待世界的一种模板——Mitch Prinstein即使离开学校几十年后，大多数人仍能毫不费力地回忆起年级里最受欢迎孩子的名字——比老师和同学的名字更容易记住，Prinstein在他2017年的书《受欢迎：在崇尚地位世界中讨喜的力量》中写道。而且不仅仅是记忆挥之不去。我们可能倾向于认为，一旦最后一次踏出校门，高中等级制度就变得无关紧要。但事实证明，它可能对我们施加一种奇怪而持久的控制。研究表明，我们青少年时期有多受欢迎和讨人喜欢，可以影响未来多年的生活，从我们如何理解社交互动到恋爱关系的强度、生活满意度，甚至健康。正是美国心理学家John Coie改变了研究人员对受欢迎程度的看法。他在1980年代初进行的开创性研究开始于此。

通过向学童询问关于同学的两个简单问题：你最喜欢谁？你最不喜欢谁？在数百张碎纸片上潦草的稚嫩笔迹中，科伊得以勾勒出关于人类社会行为的新见解。你可能会认为，孩子们要么被同伴普遍喜欢，要么被普遍讨厌。事实上，科伊和他的同事发现，孩子可能同时被不同学生喜欢和讨厌，或者既不被喜欢也不被讨厌。有些孩子被同伴频繁提及——他们高度显眼，如同小名人。另一些则几乎无人提及。科伊首次利用孩子们的答案提出了五种社会类别。“被接纳者”和“被排斥者”分别指被广泛喜欢或讨厌的人；“争议者”指同时获得大量“喜欢”和“讨厌”票数的人；“被忽视者”指几乎不被提及、无论好坏的人；而“普通者”则指在任何方向上都不极端的儿童（尽管大多数人倾向于某一类别）。许多研究证实了这些标签的实用性。它们通常发现，约40%的孩子属于“普通者”，60%则归入其余四类之一。最受欢迎的孩子往往被同伴视为善良、鼓励和支持他人，而“被忽视者”则倾向于安静和退缩。“被排斥者”可能具有攻击性并欺凌他人，或缺乏自信、社交焦虑且自身成为欺凌受害者。“争议者”是最罕见的群体，他们分化了人群——通常被视为班级小丑或叛逆者。值得注意的是，科伊发现，当孩子们被引入新的同伴群体时，他们的标签在很大程度上保持不变。尽管最初的研究针对小学生，但许多研究在青少年中复制了这些发现。其中一项研究发现，约一半的孩子在五年后升入高中时，仍保持着小学时的标签。“我在小学有过非常糟糕的经历，我总记得妈妈对我说‘上高中会好起来的’，”我询问高中经历的另一位朋友康妮*说。“但我认为，一旦你被欺凌过，或者你有什么让你明显与众不同……就像我成了容易下手的目标。”高中头几个月因各种原因（包括在一所白人为主的学校中身为混血儿）成为欺凌目标后，康妮转了学。然而，在新学校，她很快遇到了类似的模式。（了解新发现的对抗欺凌的有力方法。）虽然标签保持不变，但小学和高中之间的社会动态发生了显著变化。在小学，“受欢迎”的孩子仅仅是那些最被喜欢的——往往是那些

##段落

那些乖巧听话、学业优异的孩子，因为在那个阶段，孩子的价值观通常与成年监护人一致。到了高中，情况就变了。成年人及其所代表的一切都变得令人遗憾地不受待见。一个认真尽责的优等生可能会发现自己被归入“书呆子”行列，而一个更吵闹、更具争议性的孩子，其声望却可能意外地如日中天。

我打电话给曾几何时的操场小霸王、如今已是我密友的乔治娅，问她是否觉得自己在高中时很受欢迎。她告诉我她从不这样想自己。“‘受欢迎’听起来好像人们喜欢你，而我不觉得我们当时一定被人喜欢，”她说，“也许更像是……臭名昭著……吵闹且爱博眼球。”作为青少年，乔治娅体现了“争议性”的原型。她行为激进，在课堂上捣乱。有多少人爱她，大概就有不少人讨厌她。我告诉她，包括我在内，人们一度都很怕她。但她认为自己因此不配“受欢迎”标签的看法是错的。

“我们开始关注谁可能获得最多关注，谁可能更强势或更‘酷’，”普林斯坦说，“那些开始变得更有外在吸引力的人，那些符合同伴规范的人，[比如]穿着得体或擅长运动的人。”参与“伪成熟”行为——即与年龄更大的青少年或成人相关的行为——是通往地位的又一条捷径。喝酒、吸毒、过早涉足恋情的青少年更可能被视为受欢迎——至少在一段时间内如此。大约在15岁左右，这种行为赋予地位的程度开始减弱。

随着高中生逐渐成熟，公开追逐地位在社会上不再那么有利，“讨人喜欢”开始重新成为社会地位的重要决定因素。但这些早期极端社会分层经历的涟漪效应可能影响深远。“我们小时候的经历——是否被人喜欢、是否受欢迎或地位高——似乎对我们产生持久的影响，甚至40年后依然如此，”普林斯坦说，“讨人喜欢和地位高有着截然相反的影响。讨人喜欢是好的，它通常会带来各种积极健康、工作、学业和心理上的成果。”

“而地位高实际上会导致相反的结果。”研究人员曾将高中文化视为成人社会的不成熟版本。到了20世纪60年代，他们开始明白这种“同伴文化”要奇怪得多——一个由自身异想天开的迷恋和一套套规则驱动的平行世界。高中社交图景并非简单的等级制度，而是一个由小团体构成的动态系统。关键原型反复出现。

从美国派到早餐俱乐部，流行文化中充斥着各种青少年群体：受欢迎的学生、叛逆者、被排斥者和书呆子。在高中最初的几年里，这些小团体之间的界限往往十分严格。德裔美国精神分析学家埃里克·埃里克森在他1959年的著作《身份与生命周期》中写道：“年轻人可能会变得异常抱团、偏狭和残忍，排斥那些‘与众不同’的人。”这是一种人类现象，有些人比他人获得更多的社会权力和支配地位。而在青春期，这种现象尤为突出——露西·福克斯认为，这种偏狭可能是“一种必要的防御”，用以抵御童年身份丧失带来的冲击，加之荷尔蒙变化的神秘侵袭，以及未来充满各种可能性和选择所带来的压倒性压力。他提出，青少年通过“形成小团体和自我标签化”来帮助彼此度过这种不适。这种自我分类使青少年更容易在社交世界中游刃有余，因为每个人的相对“类别”决定了他们应如何被对待。

然而，流行文化中常被忽视的一点是，大量青少年并不属于任何特定的亚文化群体。1985年的一项研究发现，约45%的高中生仅将自己定义为“普通人”。受欢迎的学生声称自己注重外表和派对，而自我定义为“普通人”的学生则会说“我只是个普通青少年”。被视为“不正常”或因错误原因而突出，可能带来社交灾难。康妮回忆道，她13岁来到新学校时，发现很难在滑溜的社交阶梯上站稳脚跟。她描述了自己尝试放大不同特质以寻找合适小团体的过程。

她说：“我记得试过和书呆子女孩做朋友，也试过和酷女孩交朋友。我会说，‘哦，我真的很爱读书，所有作业都做。’但那一套行不通，于是我就改说，‘哦，我化妆，我打理头发’之类的话。我还试着融入搞音乐的人群，开始学吹小号。”但这一切都徒劳无功。她说：“我想心里明白这根本不奏效，没有我能融入的位置。到最后，我完全被大家忽视了。”在高中临近结束时，这种严苛的社会等级会稍微松动。20世纪90年代初，研究员大卫·金尼开展了一项民族志研究项目，他深入一所高中，近距离观察小团体界限的变化。他追踪了那些从前是“书呆子”的学生，发现他们成功转型为“普通人”。早期高中小团体的严格性可能反映了年轻人有限的认知能力。

在青春期，他指出，虽然年轻青少年日益能够自我反思，但许多人无法区分自己思考自己的频率（很多）与他人思考自己的频率。对于金尼采访的许多年轻“书呆子”来说，这导致了令人衰弱的自我关注和社交互动中的瘫痪。最终，持续的认知发展使昔日的书呆子能够减少恐惧，并围绕自己建立提供积极反馈的同龄人群体。随着青少年成熟，从众的束缚开始松动。受欢迎的孩子甚至可能面临另类、叛逆类型的威胁。金尼的研究发现，在后期，“时尚派”受到“外表怪异、行为喧闹”的学生挑战，这些学生“与他们争夺全校人气”。其中一些微妙的转变在我15岁时乔治娅第一次邀请我出去玩时可能已经悄然发生，但我仍然记得当时的困惑和难以置信。那时，我是一个以男性为主的“瘾君子”群体的成员。乔治娅是想对我开某种恶作剧吗？我会不会被引诱出去，然后以某种方式受到羞辱？差不多20年后，我问乔治娅为什么想和我做朋友，这是我以前从未问过她的问题。我在想，是我哪些闪光特质吸引了她的注意——是我的机智，还是我的魅力？“我想是我们都有某种古怪之处，”她犹豫地说。“比如，我们谁都不正常。”鉴于高中生活种种独特的怪癖，令人瞩目的是我们多么频繁地用高中作为成人互动的参照框架。英国牛津大学心理学家、著有《成年：青春期如何塑造我们》一书的露西·福克斯在社交媒体上分享了一篇关于“刻薄女孩”效应的帖子后，收到了大量共鸣回应。“很多人说，不只是青少年，我在工作场所也看到这种情况……我在学校门口的妈妈们身上也看到这种情况，”福克斯说。“这是一种人类现象，有些人获得更多的社会权力和他人的支配地位。只是在青春期尤为明显。”福克斯指出，青少年几乎每天与相同的人相处多年，这种方式“在成年期基本不会发生，除了军队或监狱。环境的强度超越了大脑内部发生的事情。”正是这种强度部分解释了为什么这些经历深植于我们心中，塑造我们未来多年对社交遭遇的理解方式，普林斯坦说。“我们会唤起14岁时的那些经历，作为看待世界的模板，”普林斯坦说。他引用的研究表明，我们所使用的心理模式

我们处理社会世界的能力始于童年时期，而当人们思考社会行为时，大脑中处理记忆的部分会变得活跃。“那些记忆一直在被重新唤起。”我们中的许多人可能都曾好奇，青少年时期认识的“酷孩子”后来怎么样了。在2015年的一项研究中，美国弗吉尼亚大学心理学教授约瑟夫·艾伦试图寻找答案。他的发现对曾经受欢迎的年轻人来说并不是个好兆头。艾伦跟踪调查了美国东南部184名年龄从13岁到23岁的青少年，发现那些在青春期早期追求地位、表现出伪成熟行为的年轻人，在亲密关系和犯罪行为方面面临长期困难的风险更大。早期接触酒精和毒品与日后更容易出现药物滥用和成瘾问题有关。而早期对地位的关注会导致人际关系浅薄，难以维持友谊和浪漫关系。被拒绝的经历也会留下伤痕。普林斯坦的研究发现，被拒绝的高中生可能会随着时间的推移变得更加抑郁。他假设存在一个负面反馈循环，即被拒绝的经历会导致更多的退缩，这反过来又加剧了被拒绝的感觉。人们完全可以扭转局面。问题是我们没有花太多时间讨论这个话题——米奇·普林斯坦相比之下，高中时期及总体上的“讨人喜欢”——即“被接受”——是积极生活结果（如成功的职业、良好的健康和稳固的人际关系）的最强预测因素之一，甚至超过了智力和社会经济背景等因素。尽管如此，经历被拒绝的人也能培养重要的优势，比如更擅长识别他人的感受，或更敏锐地察觉他人受到不公平对待。这种情商已被证明有助于处理个人关系和工作环境。而且，孩子不必“被接受”才能在成年后享受充实的社交生活。研究发现，即使青少年时期只有一两个好朋友，也能产生保护作用，并加强未来的关系。最重要的是，我们有能力改变早期经历对我们的影响。根据普林斯坦的说法，我们在高中时期形成的社交脚本可能会成为自我实现的预言。“当我们进入社交环境时，可能会关注那些确认我们最糟糕预期的信息，”他说，“然后我们会以可能实际促进更多负面经历的方式行事。”通过选择更新这些框架——例如，决定改变对社交互动的看法——我们可以打破这种循环，创造更积极的社交结果。

对同伴一句模棱两可的评论可能并非有意让我们不快——我们可以帮助自己获得更有价值的体验，他说。作为一位曾经“高地位”的青少年，格鲁吉亚从小就有冒险、伪成熟的行为，她说：“我对年轻的自己有些悲伤，因为我从未体验过仅仅做一个普通孩子是什么感觉。”她告诉我，早年目睹朋友被打，加上家中虐待行为，让她确信要表现得咄咄逼人，以显得刀枪不入。  
更多类似内容：• 自嘲的好处与陷阱 • 我们的性格有多少是天生决定的？ • 我如何在六周内改变性格  
她感叹自己在那时没有得到更多支持，反而被老师定型为“坏孩子”。“这完全塑造了我的职业轨迹，以及我对弱势群体的强烈倡导，”她说。  
与此同时，康妮表示，她早期的被拒绝经历最终演变成一种自我破坏的模式。“我觉得自己在很多方面都放弃了自己，有太多自我毁灭的行为，以至于后来很难维持友谊，”她说。这在她青春期后期达到危机顶峰，此后她努力疗愈。十多年后，她已经找到了自己热爱的事物——包括一项创作实践和一份有意义的职业——并表示她很少再想起高中时光。  
康妮和格鲁吉亚都证明了，我们在高中时被贴上的标签不必成为终身判决。“人们完全可以扭转局面，”普林斯坦同意。“问题在于我们很少谈论这一点——这意味着我们更容易重蹈覆辙。”  
* 姓名已更改。  
——如需值得信赖的健康与福祉洞察，请订阅Health Fix通讯，由资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写，她也是Live Well For Longer和Six Steps to Calm课程的作者。欲了解更多BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。

readings.title: 'Brutal' toll of war on Dubai's tourist trade
body: 2 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sameer Hashmi Last year Dubai welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally, but the US-Israel war with Iran has had a devastating impact on visitor numbers, and local businesses are struggling. On most evenings, Dubai's restaurants would usually be packed, with the constant buzz of diners, of tourists and residents filling tables across the city. But over the past month, many of those tables have sat empty. For Natasha Sideris, the shift has been sudden and stark. She opened her first restaurant in Dubai in 2014. Over the past decade, her Tashas hospitality group has grown to 14 outlets across the country, employing more than 1,000 people. But the US-Israel war with Iran is now taking a heavy toll on her business. Sideris says many of her restaurants, which are popular with both residents and expats, have seen revenues fall by more than 50%. But outlets that depend heavily on tourists have been hit much harder, with declines of 70% to 80%. The crisis has forced her to cut salaries by 30% for all staff including herself. "The current situation is brutal," she says. "I had a choice – either fire 30% of my staff or cut salaries to save jobs. I chose the latter for now." Sideris adds that the impact would have been worse if many of her outlets were not located inside community malls and close to residential neighbourhoods, where they still rely on local customers. The current tough reality is playing out across much of Dubai's restaurant sector. One senior executive at a restaurant chain, who asked not to be named, said footfall at its outlets has dropped to just 15-20% of normal, forcing them to place more than half of staff on unpaid leave. "We have no option," he says. "We've already shut down a few outlets temporarily, and the rest are operating with minimal staff." The impact is not limited to restaurants. The entire tourism ecosystem – from hotels and travel agencies, to transport companies and airlines – is feeling the strain. Over the past two decades, Dubai has built itself into one of the world's leading tourism hubs. Last year, the emirate welcomed 19.59 million international visitors, making it one of the most-visited cities globally. But since the war began, that momentum has been sharply disrupted. The wider UAE has come under repeated attacks, with Dubai among the key targets of Iran's military response following US and Israeli strikes. Authorities say more than 2,400 missiles and drones have been launched towards the UAE, targeting airports, ports and civilian areas, including hotels and residential buildings. More than 90% of them were intercepted and destroyed, officials say. But some debris has fallen across parts of Dubai, including major residential areas, hotels and the airport. Images of fragments striking the Fairmont hotel on the upscale Palm Island were circulated widely online. To date, 11 people have been killed and more than 185 injured across the UAE, according to authorities in the country. The conflict, which began on 28 February, has disrupted air travel across the region. In the early weeks, tens of thousands of visitors were stranded before being evacuated on special flights. Thousands of regular, scheduled flights have been cancelled since the conflict began, bringing one of the region's busiest travel hubs to a halt at times. Dubai International Airport – the world's busiest for international passengers – handled 95.2 million travellers last year.  Some operations have since resumed, with flag-carrier Emirates operating a reduced flight schedule while working to restore full network operations. But with tourists leaving and the number of new arrivals collapsing, hotel stays in Dubai have fallen steeply. Occupancy levels across Dubai hotels dropped to between 15% and 20% of the usual level for this time of the year in the weeks following the outbreak of the war, according to Mamoun Hmiden, chief business officer at travel booking firm Wego. Hotels have responded with deep discounts, particularly during the Eid period, in an attempt to attract residents. Some luxury properties on Palm Jumeirah, one of the city's premium hotel hubs, have cut prices by as much as half. "The uncertainty is disrupting everyone at the moment," says Hmiden. Some hospitality chains have temporarily shut down some properties or closed certain sections, citing scheduled renovations – a move typically seen during the quieter summer months. A senior executive at an international hospitality group said occupancy at some properties had fallen to single digits. "It made sense to cut operational costs by shutting down for a few weeks and reviewing the situation later," he says. Even business hotels are under pressure. Dubai, a major hub for conferences and events, has seen organisers cancel or postpone large gatherings in the coming months. Majestic Hotels, which operates around 450 rooms across three properties, says occupancy has dropped to record lows. "We are seeing cancellations beyond April," says Varun Raj, cluster director of sales and marketing. "A lot of events have been cancelled, making it difficult for travellers to plan ahead." The slowdown comes after several years of rapid growth. During the Covid-19 pandemic, Dubai was among the first destinations to reopen to international visitors, allowing its tourism sector to recover faster than many global peers. Since then, it has expanded into a broader and more diversified market – strengthening its position as a luxury destination, while also attracting large numbers of mid-market and price-sensitive travellers from regions such as South Asia, Europe and the former Soviet states. That surge in demand has been matched by a sharp increase in supply. Years of growth have driven expansion not only in hotel capacity, but also in short-term apartment rentals across the city. That additional supply is now under pressure. Data firm AirDNA shared that a little over 226,500 short-term bookings were cancelled across the UAE between February 28 to March 29, the first month since the war began.   The downturn is also being felt by the migrant workforce that form the backbone of Dubai's hospitality industry – from restaurant staff to hotel workers.  As demand weakens, many have seen their hours reduced, or they have been placed on unpaid leave. While the UAE's labour system allows companies to adjust quickly to changing conditions, that flexibility can leave workers exposed to sudden income losses. "It feels like we are back to the Covid-19 period," says a South Asian waiter working at a high-end restaurant. There are fears we could lose our jobs again and be forced to go back home." He and several colleagues have been placed on unpaid leave, with no clarity on when – or if – they will return to work. Some hotels, including five-star properties, have started laying off employees. Rights groups say many migrant workers in the UAE are already financially vulnerable, with some carrying debt linked to recruitment fees. The impact of the war is also being felt across the wider Middle East. Research by Tourism Economics, part of Oxford Economics, suggests that between 23 million and 38 million fewer people could travel to the region this year, depending on how long the conflict continues. Between $34bn (£25bn) and $56bn in visitor spending could be lost. "If the war ends soon, there could be a quick recovery," says Hmiden. "But if it drags on, we have to start questioning the entire summer season." This week – Dubai announced $272.26 million in support for businesses, including tourism, over the next three to six months. Hotels will be allowed to delay sales-related fees and tourism dirham charges – a fee applied to guests staying in the city.  Authorities in Dubai are also working on plans to revive tourism once the conflict subsides, including new campaigns and promotional offers.  "The war is out of our control," says one official. "But we are preparing for when it ends." More like this: • How the Iran war is affecting global travel • How a prolonged Middle East conflict could reshape how we fly • Is Dubai's glossy image under threat? Sideris is hoping that landlords will provide rent relief in the form of deferred payments or reduced payments for the time being to support local businesses. For Sideris, the outlook remains uncertain. She says a recovery is possible from October if the war ends soon. But if the conflict continues, the timeline could shift to next year – bringing the risk of layoffs and outlet closures. "We've got enough cash to see us through a month or two... maximum three, and then past that, what do we do? After that, we will have to take tougher calls. Hopefully not. And this insanity ends soon." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. 2026年4月2日 分享 保存 设为Google首选 Sameer Hashmi 去年迪拜接待了1959万国际游客，使其成为全球访问量最大的城市之一，但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争对游客人数造成了毁灭性影响，当地企业正苦苦挣扎。在大多数夜晚，迪拜的餐厅通常座无虚席，食客、游客和居民的持续喧嚣填满了整个城市的餐桌。但过去一个月，许多餐桌都空置了。对Natasha Sideris来说，这种转变突然而明显。她于2014年在迪拜开了第一家餐厅。过去十年里，她的Tashas餐饮集团已发展到全国14家门店，雇佣超过1000名员工。但美国-以色列与伊朗的战争现在正对她的生意造成沉重打击。Sideris表示，她许多受居民和外籍人士欢迎的餐厅收入下降了超过50%。但严重依赖游客的门店受到的冲击要大得多，降幅达70%到80%。这场危机迫使她将所有员工（包括她自己）的工资削减30%。她说：“目前的情况很残酷。我面临一个选择——要么解雇30%的员工，要么削减工资以保住工作。我暂时选择了后者。”Sideris补充说，如果她的许多门店不是位于社区商场内且靠近居民区，依赖当地客户，影响会更糟。目前严峻的现实正席卷迪拜大部分餐饮行业。一家连锁餐厅的高管（要求匿名）表示，其门店客流量已降至正常的15-20%，迫使他们让超过一半员工无薪休假。他说：“我们别无选择。我们已经暂时关闭了几家门店，其余门店以最少员工运营。”影响不仅限于餐厅。整个旅游生态系统——从酒店和旅行社，到运输公司和航空公司——都感受到压力。过去二十年，迪拜已将自己打造成世界领先的旅游中心之一。去年，该酋长国接待了1959万国际游客，使其成为全球访问量最大的城市之一。但自战争开始以来，这一势头被急剧打断。更广泛的阿联酋遭受了反复攻击，在美国和以色列打击后，迪拜是伊朗军事回应的主要目标之一。当局表示，超过2400枚导弹和无人机被发射向阿联酋，瞄准机场、港口和民用区域，包括酒店和住宅建筑。官员称，其中超过90%被拦截并摧毁。但一些碎片已落在迪拜部分地区，包括

主要住宅区、酒店和机场。高档棕榈岛上费尔蒙酒店遭碎片撞击的画面在网上广泛传播。据阿联酋当局称，截至目前，该国已有11人死亡，超过185人受伤。这场始于2月28日的冲突已扰乱整个地区的航空旅行。最初几周，数万名游客被困，随后通过特别航班撤离。自冲突爆发以来，数千个常规定期航班被取消，有时导致该地区最繁忙的旅行枢纽之一陷入停滞。迪拜国际机场——全球国际旅客吞吐量最大的机场——去年接待了9520万人次旅客。部分运营已恢复，旗舰航空公司阿联酋航空正在缩减航班计划，同时努力恢复全面网络运营。但随着游客离开和新抵达人数骤降，迪拜的酒店入住率大幅下滑。据旅行预订公司Wego的首席商务官马蒙·赫米登称，战争爆发后的几周内，迪拜各酒店的入住率降至往年同期正常水平的15%至20%。酒店纷纷推出大幅折扣，尤其是在开斋节期间，以吸引本地居民。朱美拉棕榈岛——该市高端酒店聚集地之一——的一些豪华物业已将价格削减近一半。赫米登表示：“目前的不确定性扰乱了每个人的计划。”一些酒店连锁集团以计划内翻新为由，暂时关闭部分物业或某些区域——此举通常在较为淡季的夏季出现。一家国际酒店集团的高级高管表示，部分物业的入住率已降至个位数。他说：“关闭几周以降低运营成本，之后再评估情况，这样做是合理的。”即使是商务酒店也面临压力。迪拜是会议和活动的主要枢纽，主办方已取消或推迟未来数月的大型聚会。经营三家物业、共约450间客房的雄伟酒店表示，入住率已降至历史低点。销售与市场营销集群总监瓦伦·拉杰说：“我们看到4月之后的预订被取消。许多活动被取消，使旅行者难以提前规划。”这一放缓发生在数年快速增长之后。在新冠疫情期间，迪拜是最早向国际游客重新开放的目的地之一，使其旅游业比许多全球同行恢复得更快。此后，它扩展为更广泛、更多元化的市场——巩固了其作为豪华目的地的地位，同时

同时也吸引了大量来自南亚、欧洲和前苏联国家的中端市场和价格敏感型游客。需求的激增伴随着供应的急剧增加。多年的增长不仅推动了酒店容量的扩张，也促进了全市短期公寓租赁的发展。这些新增供应现在面临压力。数据公司AirDNA分享说，在2月28日至3月29日期间（战争开始后的第一个月），阿联酋各地有超过226,500笔短期预订被取消。这种下滑也影响到了构成迪拜酒店业骨干的移民劳动力——从餐厅员工到酒店工人。随着需求减弱，许多人工作时间减少，或被安排无薪休假。虽然阿联酋的劳动制度允许公司快速适应变化条件，但这种灵活性可能使工人面临突然的收入损失。“感觉我们回到了新冠时期，”一位在高档餐厅工作的南亚服务员说。“我们担心可能再次失业，被迫回国。”他和几位同事已被安排无薪休假，不清楚何时或是否能重返工作岗位。一些酒店，包括五星级酒店，已开始裁员。权利组织表示，阿联酋的许多移民工人已经在经济上脆弱，有些人背负着与招聘费用相关的债务。战争的影响也波及整个中东地区。牛津经济研究院旗下旅游经济学的研究表明，今年可能有2300万至3800万游客减少前往该地区，具体取决于冲突持续的时间。游客支出可能损失340亿至560亿美元。“如果战争迅速结束，可能会有快速复苏，”赫米登说。“但如果拖延下去，我们就必须质疑整个夏季季节。”本周，迪拜宣布在未来三到六个月内为企业（包括旅游业）提供2.7226亿美元的支持。酒店将被允许延迟支付销售相关费用和旅游迪拉姆费用——这是对入住城市游客征收的费用。迪拜当局也在制定计划，一旦冲突平息后重振旅游业，包括新活动和促销优惠。“战争超出我们的控制，”一位官员说。“但我们正在为结束做准备。”更多类似内容：•伊朗战争如何影响全球旅行•中东长期冲突如何重塑我们的飞行方式•迪拜的光鲜形象是否受到威胁？西德里希望房东能提供租金减免，形式包括延迟付款或暂时减少付款，以支持当地企业。对于西

deris，前景依然不确定。她表示，如果战争很快结束，从十月份起可能会复苏。但如果冲突持续，时间表可能推迟到明年——这带来裁员和门店关闭的风险。“我们的现金足以支撑一两个月……最多三个月，之后我们该怎么办？之后，我们将不得不做出更艰难的决定。希望不会如此，希望这种疯狂能很快结束。”——如需面向董事会及更广泛领域的最新洞察与专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》新闻简报，而《必读清单》则提供精选专题和见解。欲了解更多商业及更多内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。 商业 战争 新闻 专题 伊朗 战争 商业世界

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

##段落
处理焦虑的聪明方法——源自足球巨星莱昂内尔·梅西

2023年6月22日 / 亚当·阿尔特博士 / Facebook / X / LinkedIn / Reddit / WhatsApp / 黛博拉·斯皮尔曼

是什么将世界顶尖人物与其余70亿人区分开来？

非凡的才华往往看起来像一场革命——一个人以从未有过的方式做事——但许多革命性的才华实际上建立在渐进式微调的基础上。这些微调随时间发展，常常弥补那些可能击垮普通人才的弱点和焦虑。

然而，尽管梅西才华横溢，他却以焦虑著称。多年来，他在重要比赛前习惯性地在球场上呕吐。

以世界最佳足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西获得的金球奖（授予年度最佳足球运动员的奖项）比任何其他球员都多。他在一个日历年内的进球数超过任何其他现役球员，是西班牙西甲联赛的历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今最高的进球率，几乎每场比赛都能进球。

然而，尽管他光芒四射，他却以焦虑闻名。多年来，梅西习惯性地在重大比赛前在球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利之后，另一位已故的阿根廷足球巨擘迭戈·马拉多纳不客气地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前去二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。

拥有惊人天赋并不能让你免受焦虑的困扰，而世界上许多顶尖人物恰恰因为对自己期望过高而深陷焦虑。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱自己的才华，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，这种机制同时也是他战术智慧背后的秘密。

梅西在开场几分钟内会做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。第二，他观察对手。

一场足球比赛持续90分钟（外加几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就积极参与比赛。哨声一响，他们就恳求队友传球，执行教练在赛前布置的战术。

但梅西以在开场几分钟内不参与比赛而闻名。这是他的渐进式微调，随着他在越来越高的水平上比赛而逐渐形成。在开场几分钟里，梅西在中场附近来回踱步，几乎不与队友互动。其他球员在奔跑，有时甚至冲刺，而梅西大部分时间在走路，很少超过慢跑的速度。

梅西在开场几分钟内会做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。慢慢进入比赛状态是梅

ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间内保持完全投入的方式。他在场上呕吐的问题已经自行解决，部分原因可能是他找到了一种更有效的镇定神经的方法。其次，他利用这段时间观察对手。他的双腿移动缓慢，但双眼在球员间快速扫视，评估对手的优势、劣势和战术，同时监控己方球队在持球和无球状态下的跑动。梅西在比赛初期对球队的价值较低，但这种战术性的停顿提升了他在剩余95%比赛时间里的价值。

如果将足球比赛划分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西高度依赖准备。在2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那对阵宿敌皇家马德里的一场经典比赛中，梅西在整场90分钟里只跑了4分钟，走了超过80分钟。然而，当他投入时，他充满活力，创造了9次机会，打入1球，并助攻队友再进1球。

正如你可能想象的，停顿比听起来更难。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

这种模式对梅西并不罕见，而且往往在最重大的比赛中，他会强化自己的赛中准备。这种准备也解释了他为何能一次又一次在正确的时间出现在正确的地点。尽管他的位置感看似超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他逐分钟学习到，某个特定的后卫会留下某块特定的球场区域无人防守，或者当两名中场球员向中场中路靠拢时，会留出球场的一小块空当。

对我们其他人的启示很明确：当你感到焦虑时，无论是在体育运动中还是在更广泛的生活中，请停顿。慢下来。做准备。

正如你可能想象的，停顿比听起来更难。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。贾德森·布鲁尔，一位精神病学家和神经科学家，职业生涯的大部分时间都在思考如何“什么都不做”。

大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

他的方法指导成瘾者在渴望来袭时，通过遵循四个步骤来抵抗焦虑的浪潮，这套方法的首字母缩写为RAIN：

识别（Recognize）正在升起的感受。

允许（Allow）它存在。

探究（Investigate）你的情绪和想法（例如，“我身体现在发生了什么？”）

留意（Note）每时每刻正在发生的事情。

布鲁尔曾表示，他的方法灵感来自临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫。为测试该方法，布鲁尔与努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾以顽固著称——比许多在用户身上产生更强即时反应的硬性毒品更难戒除。

在释放该项目之前——

在吸烟者身上，布鲁尔想在自己身上测试这一系统。问题在于，“我是个不吸烟者，”布鲁尔写道，“却需要与那些觉得不抽烟脑袋就要爆炸的患者感同身受。”
尼古丁的半衰期大约为两小时，因此起初，吸烟者需要每次抵抗住两小时不点烟的冲动。布鲁尔推断，能坚持两小时不吸烟的吸烟者会培养出新的不吸烟习惯，逐步延长这些时段，直到他们完全不再感到吸烟的冲动。
他通过练习连续两小时静坐冥想不动来模拟这些抵抗期。在坐立不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、注意——如果他动了身体，计时器就会重置，他必须重新开始。
这听起来可能容易，但两小时不娱乐地静坐是一段很长的时间。“令人惊讶的是，长时间不动带来的身体疼痛并没有难倒我，”布鲁尔写道，“是那种不安……那些渴望叫喊着：‘起来！’”
几个月后，当大多数接受其他治疗计划的病人复发时，他的正念小组保持干净状态。
连续多月，布鲁尔都会接近目标，然后被不安击败。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两小时……之后每次静坐都越来越容易，因为我有信心能做到。而且我知道我的病人能戒烟。他们只需要合适的工具。”
布鲁尔是对的。他的病人曾被困住，无法戒掉地球上最令人上瘾的物质之一。但当他进行一项又一项研究，将他的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法对比时，他的方法有效性超过两倍。
几个月后，当大多数接受其他治疗计划的病人复发时，他的正念小组保持干净状态。他们戒除瘾症的可能性高出五倍以上，用的方法本质上教会他们在身体最迫切驱使他们行动的时刻暂停。
在布鲁尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许是最关键的。让一种体验冲刷过你听起来出奇容易，因为它不需要你做任何事。但这正是关键所在。它之所以困难，是因为尽管有行动的冲动，你却被迫什么都不做。
尽管暂停和准备有诸多好处，但有时主事件并不按计划进行。梅西输过无数场比赛，而布鲁尔的尼古丁成瘾者并非全都在实验结束数周或数月后仍然保持戒断。掌握这些失败后的焦虑和不适至关重要，这是主要挑战之一。

取得突破的人与长期陷入困境的人之间的主要差异。
